power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The striking constraints of some human cognitive processes stand in stark contrast to the near limitless capability of others.

While we can acquire and flexibly use vast amounts of information, the amount we can process at any one time is often stiflingly limited: for example the number of items we can hold in working memory or the number of tasks that can be performed at once.
Here, we integrate ideas from information theory, cognitive science, and neuroscience to offer a unified account of why processing is often so limited.

We argue that this reflects a fundamental tradeoff between generalization-how effectively existing representations can be used in novel settings-and how many distinct representations can be processed in parallel.

Representations that best promote strong forms of generalization -a characteristically human cognitive strength -come at the expense of surprisingly strict limits in the number of items that can be processed at once, an equally characteristic human weakness.
We refer to this as the "curse of generalization."
We formulate this first in information-theoretic terms, and then in process models, including a neural network model of classic tasks used to demonstrate strict limits in human processing capacity.

This tension offers a potential explanation for a range of phenomena -from performance on the tasks on which we focus, to representational learning and skill acquisition more broadly -as well as the performance of modern machine learning architectures that exhibit generalization capabilities comparable to humans.
Although humans exhibit striking information processing capabilities, they can often also be strikingly limited.
Most famously, humans can actively maintain only a handful of items in mind at one time, an observation familiar from both everyday experience and classic laboratory experiments.

For example, it has long been recognized that we are generally limited to remembering only about 7 randomly presented digits at a given time (e.g., Hayes, 1952), and even fewer when rehearsal and chunking are prevented (Cowan, 2001).
text.formatted: For example, it has long been recognized that we are generally limited to remembering only about 7 randomly presented digits at a given time (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Hayes, 1952)</ref>, and even fewer when rehearsal and chunking are prevented <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Cowan, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Remarkably, however, the causes of this limit remain poorly understood.

While the resources necessary to carry out human cognitive function are clearly finite -e.g., storage space (Amit, 1989), processing time (Cheyette and Piantadosi, 2020), and the precision of neuronal signaling (Ma et al., 2014) -it is unclear why limits in these resources alone should impose such severe cognitive constraints, especially given the precision with which we can process information in many instances, the tremendous volume of information we can store and retrieve from longer term memory (Brady et al., 2008), and the vast resources available to the human brain (over 100 billion neurons, that consume approximatelyfoot_0 3 of the body's energy).

text.text: Furthermore, it is unclear why these strict constraints are so similar across diverse forms of representation and types of cognitive processes.

This diversity was the focus of George Miller's classic article (1956), in which he observed that the limit to the number of items -seven plus or minus two -that can be held in immediate memory (now more commonly referred to as "short term" or "working memory") is remarkably similar to limits in the amount of information -about 2.5 bits -that can be processed in other tasks, including perceptual ones such as matching a tone to one of several reference tones (Gravetter and Lockhead, 1973; Nizami, 2010; Pollack, 1952), or estimating the number of items in a visual display (Cheyette and Piantadosi, 2020; Kaufman et al., 1949; Mandler and Shebo, 1982).

text.text: The similarity of these constraints intrigued Miller, but he was perplexed by several factors: the disparity of information and tasks involved; the fact that seven "items" can carry substantially more than 2.5 bits of information (e.g., a decimal digit carries more than one bit of information); and the lack of any principles or processing mechanisms that could explain the relationship between these constraints.

Accordingly, he could not convince himself that the prevalence of the "magical number seven" was more than a "Pythagorean coincidence," a provocative conclusion that has continued to attract attention in the decades since (e.g., Shiffrin and Nosofsky, 1994).

text.text: Here we reconsider Miller's conclusion, by identifying a fundamental principle of information processing that puts the use of overlapping, or shared representations in tension with the use of distinct, or separated representations 1 .

We show that this tension, coupled with the value of shared representations for generalization, can explain the severe processing limits observed across disparate cognitive domains -limits that fall consistently within range of Miller's "magical number seven" -when the tasks involved require generalization, and may provide a normative basis for the role of serial processing and cognitive control that are signature characteristics of human cognitive function in many settings.

Our argument is as follows: In general, increasing the complexity of a representational system (quantified as the number of bits available) increases the amount of information the system can represent; that is, its expressivity.

In principle, this can also increase the amount of information that can be actively processed and kept distinct at the same time -a quantity that we refer to as processing capacity, in alignment with the question that interested Miller.

However, increasing complexity is not the sole determinant of processing capacity; critically, it is also strongly impacted by the structure of the representations and, most importantly, how they relate to one another.

Our primary observations are that: i) there is a fundamental tension between generalization and processing capacity; ii) this tension depends on the presence of uncertainty in the decision process (as elaborated below); iii) the nature of this tension is such that optimizing representations for generalizationthat is, the use of shared, or similar representations to represent correspondingly similar items -limits their ability to be reliably distinguished, thereby constraining the number of items that can be processed at the same time and thus limits processing capacity.
In this article, we formalize and examine this tension between generalization and processing capacity.

We build on the well-established tradeoff in information theory between compression and accuracy-grounded in Rate-Distortion Theory (RDT) and the Information Bottleneck Shannon, 1959; Tishby et al., 2000-and on its relationship to principles of generalization.

text.text: In prior work, the capacity constraint motivating the need for compression is generally taken as given, though it remains unclear why capacity should be so severely limited in the first place.

This question arises at two levels: what constrains expressivity, the precision with which a single item can be represented (e.g., Sims, 2018); and, more broadly, what constrains processing capacity, the number of items that can be represented and kept distinct at the same time (Bays & Husain, 2008; Cheyette & Piantadosi, 2020; Ma et al., 2014; Sims, 2016).

text.text: Here, rather than assuming that multi-item capacity is set by intrinsic resource constraints (e.g., structural or metabolic), as in traditional theories of attention, working memory, and cognitive control (Anderson, 1983; Cowan, 2001; Posner & Snyder, 1975; Shiffrin & Schneider, 1977), we consider a reversal of the logic: if representations are optimized for generalization, to what extent can this account for the constraints on processing capacity?

text.text: Specifically, we show that optimizing representational compression for generalization imposes remarkably strict constraints on processing capacity -ones that align with the constraints observed in tasks that involve the processing of novel stimuli and thus rely on generalization, including those considered by Miller (1956).

text.text: We suggest that this tension between generalization and processing capacity, and the severity of the attendant effects, reflects a fundamental principle of its own, that we refer to as the Miller-Shepard Law.

We formalize this relationship using two kinds of tasks: an identification task, requiring selection of an item in a reference set that is identical to a probe, that evaluates the ability to distinguish among items; and a generalization task, requiring selection of the item most similar to the probe that is not identical to any item in the set, and thus relies on similarity-based representations.

We quantify the impact that the degree of similarity among representations (parameterized as a generalization gradient) and number of items in the reference set (as a measure of processing capacity) have on performance in each type of task.
We find a robust and strikingly severe tension between generalization and processing capacity in the identification and generalization tasks.

Importantly, we find that this tension appears only when there is uncertainty in the decision process used to identify an item and/or relate it to others: With no uncertainty, both identification and, perhaps surprisingly, generalization are optimized by the narrowest possible generalization gradient, an explanation for which we provide with the formal analysis in Section 3.4.
However, with even vanishingly small amounts of uncertainty, the effect of the generalization gradient on performance aligns with intuition: for identification, the narrowest gradient remains best.

However, for generalization the relationship becomes non-monotonic: too narrow and there is insufficient generalization, too broad and everything is treated as the same, with an intermediate yielding the best generalization performance.
We find that this holds across multiple potential sources of processing uncertainty, including additive decision noise, superposition of representations, and dynamic retrieval processes.

Critically, we find that -owing to the log-log relationship between generalization and identification -the optimal value of the gradient for generalization is consistently associated with Draconian constraints on identification performance and thus processing capacity, restricting the latter to levels within range of the ∼2.5-bit limits famously observed by Miller.

Based on these observations, we argue that the severity of constraints in the tasks on which Miller focused was because, by design, they demanded the use of generalizable representations to process novel stimuli, which by construction involve representational sharing that, in turn, limits the number of items that can be actively represented and kept distinct at the same time.

More generally, we conclude that the severe capacity limits observed in performance on tasks designed to probe the mechanisms responsible for flexibility of processing (such as attention, working memory and cognitive control) emerge not from the resource limitations intrinsic to such systems (e.g., a fixed biological limit on storage capacity or energetic requirements per se), but because the representational compression required for generalization, and the flexibility it affords, are in fundamental tension with the ability to preserve exact information.

The remainder of the article is structured as follows: First we present the argument in a more extended form, providing additional background -including its relationship to the foundational work in information theory, semanticity and generalization on which it is based, and an illustrative example of the problem.
(We elaborate the constructs, and the assumptions on which they are based, in Appendix E).
We then provide a formal derivation of the relationship between generalization and processing capacity in information theoretic terms, focusing on 1-dimensional stimuli.

We follow this with a brief summary of results using a simple process model (described more fully in Appendix B) to simulate performance on the identification and generalization tasks with 2-dimensional stimuli, that are required to explore the effects of compositionality but that are intractable to analysis using the formal model.
Finally, we describe a mechanistic (neural network) model, parameterized using neurobiological and psychophysical data, to simulate the tasks originally considered by Miller (1956).

In the General Discussion, we consider how our information theoretic treatment aligns with Miller's original formulation of the problem; more broadly how the tradeoff between generalization and processing capacity relates to other foundational constructs in the cognitive literature, such as the theory of complementary learning systems, and how our approach may provide a normative account of cognitive control and its association with serial processing; and, finally, the implications this work has for the understanding and design of artificial neural networks.

In this section we lay out in more detail the conceptual argument that motivates the subsequent formal analyses and computational experiments, illustrating key ideas with a concrete example taken from a visual working memory paradigm.
We begin by assuming that agents seek to maximize both the scope and accuracy with which they can represent the world.
In principle, this can be done by exhaustively assigning a separate, dedicated representation to every possible state of the world, that specifies all of its features.
This is sometimes referred to as "conjunctive coding" (e.g., see Figure 7, and aligns with Shepard's 1991 notion of integral dimensions.
text.formatted: This is sometimes referred to as "conjunctive coding" (e.g., see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">7</ref>, and aligns with Shepard's 1991 notion of integral dimensions.

text.text: In informationtheoretic terms, this amounts to maximizing the complexity, or "expressivity" of the representational system.
However, this is of course impossible in the extreme.
Agents have limited time for learning, finite resources for representation and computation, and even evolution cannot anticipate all possible eventualities.
In this respect, agents face the famous curse of dimensionality (Bellman, 1957).
text.formatted: In this respect, agents face the famous curse of dimensionality <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Bellman, 1957)</ref>.

text.text: This has led investigators in statistics, cognitive science, neuroscience, and modern machine learning to search for algorithms that can efficiently acquire representations from past experience that can be applied to the broader class of experiences expected in the future.

This ability to extend the use of existing representations to represent new information -i.e., generalization -reflects a form of compression (i.e., increasing the amount of information in new settings without increasing the complexity of representation).
Although not all forms of compression necessarily support generalization (for example, randomly deleting parts of a signal), here we are interested in forms of compression that do.

Building on Rate-Distortion Theory (RDT; Shannon, 1959) and its application to efficient coding in psychology and neuroscience (e.g., Barlow, 1961; Friston, 2010; Linsker, 1988; Sims, 2016 Sims, , 2018;; Tishby et al., 2000; Zaslavsky et al., 2018), as well as work in cognitive science on the nature of representations required for generalization (e.g., Fang and Sims, 2025; Malloy and Sims, 2025; Shepard, 1987), we argue that the mature human cognitive system, through evolution and/or learning over the course of development, relies on the use of shared representations as a form of compression that supports generalization -that is, as a solution to the optimization problem of maximizing information in new settings.
text.formatted: Building on Rate-Distortion Theory (RDT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">Shannon, 1959)</ref> and its application to efficient coding in psychology and neuroscience (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Barlow, 1961;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Linsker, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">Sims, 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">Sims, , 2018;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">Tishby et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b183">Zaslavsky et al., 2018)</ref>, as well as work in cognitive science on the nature of representations required for generalization (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Fang and Sims, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Malloy and Sims, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Shepard, 1987)</ref>, we argue that the mature human cognitive system, through evolution and/or learning over the course of development, relies on the use of shared representations as a form of compression that supports generalization -that is, as a solution to the optimization problem of maximizing information in new settings.

text.text: Cognitive scientists have long highlighted two ways in which natural systems exploit representational sharing to capture structure in the world, and thereby optimize generalization, through the use of: (i) semanticity in which representations preserve the similarity structure in the world (Shepard, 1987); and (ii) compositionality, in which novel or unfamiliar states are represented through the re-combination of previously acquired represen-tations (Fodor and Pylyshyn, 1988; Shepard, 1991; Smolensky, 1990) foot_1 .
text.formatted: Cognitive scientists have long highlighted two ways in which natural systems exploit representational sharing to capture structure in the world, and thereby optimize generalization, through the use of: (i) semanticity in which representations preserve the similarity structure in the world <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">(Shepard, 1987)</ref>; and (ii) compositionality, in which novel or unfamiliar states are represented through the re-combination of previously acquired represen-tations <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Fodor and Pylyshyn, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">Shepard, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">Smolensky, 1990)</ref> <ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref> .

text.text: Together, these support generalization: Semanticity assigns similar representations to states of the world that are similar along perceptually and/or behaviorally-relevant dimensions, allowing new states that are similar to previously experienced ones to elicit similar interpretations or responses, respectively.
Compositionality allows the system to represent never-before seen states through the composition of previously acquired representations.

Together, semanticity and compositionality reflect a form of representational sharing, in which representations acquired from states of the world that have been previously experienced can be extended to represent a broader class of states that have not yet been experienced.
In this respect, they support generalization, and the characteristic flexibility of human cognitive function that this affords.
While the acquisition of shared representations supports generalization, it necessarily comes at the cost of the ability to distinguish different states.

Insofar as representational sharing reflects a form of compression (discussed below), this cost can be formalized using RDT as a reduction in accuracy, or "distortion," due to the loss of information that comes from compression.
From this, a Pareto front can be derived in the tradeoff between compression and distortion, defining a maximum achievable accuracy for a given amount of compression.

This is exemplified by the Information Bottleneck (IB; Tishby et al., 2000), which derives such a Pareto front in the amount of information preserved with respect to some task-relevant variable (e.g., a category label) as a function of compression.
text.formatted: This is exemplified by the Information Bottleneck (IB; <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">Tishby et al., 2000)</ref>, which derives such a Pareto front in the amount of information preserved with respect to some task-relevant variable (e.g., a category label) as a function of compression.

text.text: This is generally considered with regard to the processing of a single signal, or representation.
Here, we are concerned with the effect that compression has on how many representations that can be kept distinct and processed at the same time (i.e., in parallel).

As noted above, we refer to this as processing capacity -in alignment with the long tradition of interest in this feature of human cognitive function, initially brought into focus by Miller -and analyze the extent to which the distortion introduced by compression, in the service of generalization, constrains processing capacity.
text.formatted: As noted above, we refer to this as processing capacity -in alignment with the long tradition of interest in this feature of human cognitive function, initially brought into focus by <ref type="bibr">Miller -and analyze</ref> the extent to which the distortion introduced by compression, in the service of generalization, constrains processing capacity.

text.text: To the extent that compression introduces distortion one might ask why, or under what conditions, it might be advantageous for representations to be compressed?

This has typically been considered with respect to resource constraints that limit representational complexity in artificial systems (e.g., code length), and the metabolic costs of representational precision or speed of processing in biological ones (Cheyette and Piantadosi, 2020; Wilken and Ma, 2004; Zheng and Meister, 2025).
text.formatted: This has typically been considered with respect to resource constraints that limit representational complexity in artificial systems (e.g., code length), and the metabolic costs of representational precision or speed of processing in biological ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Cheyette and Piantadosi, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b180">Wilken and Ma, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b184">Zheng and Meister, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we consider another potential advantage of compression: generalization -that is, the effectiveness with which existing representations can be used to process new information, formalized as the amount of information preserved when representing novel information.
As noted above, semanticity and compositionality are forms of compression that support generalization.

For example, the form of compression (or "distortion function") used in Tishby et al. (2000) to demonstrate the IB can be thought of as a form of semantic coding (classification); and Sims (2018) shows that the exponential similarity gradient proposed by Shepard (1987) as a Universal Law of Generalization can be derived from RDT as an optimal form of compression.
text.formatted: For example, the form of compression (or "distortion function") used in <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">Tishby et al. (2000)</ref> to demonstrate the IB can be thought of as a form of semantic coding (classification); and <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">Sims (2018)</ref> shows that the exponential similarity gradient proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Shepard (1987)</ref> as a Universal Law of Generalization can be derived from RDT as an optimal form of compression.

text.text: However, as a form of compression, RDT tells us that semanticity must therefore also be associated with distortion and thus, as seen through the lens of the IB, a limit on the ability to accurately distinguish between and identify individual items.

In this article, we formally address this tradeoff between compression in the service of generalization and the costs it imposes on identification accuracy, and the dramatic impact that this has on processing capacity.

Our analyses lead to two critical observations: (i) with any amount of uncertainty in the decision process used to evaluate items, there is an intermediate amount of compression (i.e., representational sharing) that optimizes generalization; (ii) that amount of compression heavily constrains the ability to accurately identify individual items which, in turn, radically limits processing capacity (i.e., the number of items that can be processed at the same time); we refer to this as the "curse of generalization."
To make the problem concrete, consider the visual short term (or working) memory task, diagrammed in Figure 1A, that is used paradigmatically to study capacity limits in human information processing.

text.text: In this task, colored squares appear at various positions in a display, followed by a delay, and the participant's task is to determine whether the color of an item at a particular location has changed.

Performance on this task degrades precipitously when the display contains more than 4 or 5 items (see Figure 13D) -that is, within the constraints of the magical number 7 (in this case, minus two). visual display with colored squares and, following a delay, is shown either the same display or one in which the color of one of the squares has been changed at a probed location, and asked to respond whether that item is the same or different from the original display.

text.text: (B) Encoding of the information in the display as a compositional coding of semantically structured representations: Each item in the display is represented through the rapid formation of associations between feature values represented semantically along each independent feature dimension (i.e., color and position), and the display is represented through the full set of associations.
Figure 1B shows one possible scheme for how such a task might be performed.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref> shows one possible scheme for how such a task might be performed.

text.text: Each node corresponds to a representational element, with a pattern of these used to represent a feature value semantically along one of the task-relevant dimensions, and a different set of nodes dedicated to representing features along each of the two dimensions.

Importantly, in this scheme there are no nodes for combinations of feature values across dimensions: Nodes used to represent features along one dimension do not carry any information about features along the other dimension, and thus can't be used to represent the specific combination of color and location associated with a particular item.

In other words, the representations are both semantic and compositional: Representations of features along each dimension are similar for similar features (e.g., red and orange), each item is represented as a combination of its feature value along each dimension (i.e., its color and position) by associating ("binding") the representations of those features, and the display is represented as the set of associations representing each of the items in the display.
The formal structure of such semantic and compositional representations is shown graphically in Figure 7, discussed in Section 3.5, and at greater length in Appendix E.1).
text.formatted: The formal structure of such semantic and compositional representations is shown graphically in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">7</ref>, discussed in Section 3.5, and at greater length in Appendix E.1).

text.text: The use of such representational structure, and in this example compositionality in particular, confers substantial flexibility.

By representing each item as a combination of representations along different dimensions, any possible combination of feature values along those dimensions can be represented; similarly, representing displays through the combination of items allows any possible combination of items to be represented.

This scheme can also be acquired much more efficiently, since it involves learning only the representations for feature values along each dimension, which are shared across representations of different objects (i.e., combinations of features), rather than learning a separate, dedicated representation for every possible object.
Accordingly, compositional representations scale additively in the number of features, rather than multiplicatively and, in this way, mitigate the curse of dimensionality.

The representational sharing induced by semanticity (i.e., across features within dimensions) confers additional advantages for generalization, consistent with Shepard's 1987 Universal Law of Generalization, a connection that we will elaborate further in Section 3.2.
Importantly, representational sharing -whether due to semanticity and/or compositionality -introduces the risk of interference and confusion.

For example, compositionality makes it impossible to identify an item by its color if its color is the same as another item, exactly because the representations of a given feature are shared across objects.
This is exacerbated by semanticity, in which similar feature values are represented similarly along a given dimension (e.g., red and orange versus blue).

This is because similarity of representation, by construction, reduces the distance between similar representations, which makes them less distinguishable (i.e., more likely to be confused), so that even items with different feature values (e.g., red vs. orange) may now be confused.
Such similarity structure reflects a "softer" form of representational sharing (e.g., through partial overlapfoot_2 ) that, like compositional coding, introduces the risk of confusion.
text.formatted: Such similarity structure reflects a "softer" form of representational sharing (e.g., through partial overlap<ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">foot_2</ref> ) that, like compositional coding, introduces the risk of confusion.

text.text: This is consistent with a large empirical literature on similarity-based interference in short-term memory (e.g., Lewis, 1996; MacLeod, 2024).
text.formatted: This is consistent with a large empirical literature on similarity-based interference in short-term memory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Lewis, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">MacLeod, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, while supporting generalization, representational sharingwhether compositional and/or semantic -limits the reliability with which items can be distinguished from one another.
This, in turn, invokes the curse of generalization, limiting how many items can be represented distinguishably at the same time, thus constraining processing capacity.

In the sections that follow, we provide a formal, information theoretic characterization of this tension between generalization and processing capacity, that we argue may explain the pattern of constraints in human cognitive function that perplexed George Miller.

Before doing so, however, it is important to note at the outset that the tension can be managed in at least two ways: by increasing representational complexity, through the allocation of dedicated, separated representations for individual items (i.e., conjunctions of features); or by imposing serial processing.

The former can occur through forms of representational learning that transpire over longer time frames (e.g., consolidation, automatization, or chunking - Anderson, 1983; McClelland et al., 1995; Miller, 1956; Musslick et al., 2023; Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977), and can account for the near limitless capability people have for acquiring new knowledge and skills (i.e., increasingly their representational complexity) and that can also increase processing capacity.
text.formatted: The former can occur through forms of representational learning that transpire over longer time frames (e.g., consolidation, automatization, or chunking - <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Anderson, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">McClelland et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Miller, 1956;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Musslick et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977)</ref>, and can account for the near limitless capability people have for acquiring new knowledge and skills (i.e., increasingly their representational complexity) and that can also increase processing capacity.

text.text: However, these come at the cost of time (passive exposure, rehearsal, practice, etc.), and cannot account for the rapid, flexible, and effective processing of novel states, which require the use of shared representations that generalize.

The other way to overcome the risk of interference posed by shared representations is to limit how many are processed at once and, in the limit, to serialize processing. 4 From this vantage, serial processing can be viewed as acquiescing to the curse of generalization in exchange for its benefits.
text.formatted: The other way to overcome the risk of interference posed by shared representations is to limit how many are processed at once and, in the limit, to serialize processing. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">4</ref> From this vantage, serial processing can be viewed as acquiescing to the curse of generalization in exchange for its benefits.

text.text: That is the domain of function on which we focus in this article.

To cast the problem in information-theoretic terms, we assume that the knowledge required to perform a task is encoded by representations of the relevant information: observed states of the world are converted to internal representations (encoded) that are accessed for processing (in channels) to generate (transmit) a task-relevant inference and/or action (decoded) as the response.

Here, we are interested in how the structure of the internal representations impacts how much information from the original source can be transmitted to generate the task-relevant response(s) at a given time.

Specifically, we consider the degree of compression with which information is represented, implemented as the breadth of a generalization gradient, and focus on two critical factors: i) the effectiveness of generalization that can be achieved by a given degree of compression; and, given that degree of compression ii) the impact that this has on identification accuracy, and its consequences for processing capacity (i.e., how many distinct items can accurately be processed at the same without interfering with one another).

We begin by reviewing foundational work in information theory, and in particular RDT and the IB, that formalize the tradeoff between compression and identification accuracy, typically with respect to the transmission of a single signal.

We then extend this, focusing on the impact that compression -in the form of semantic and compositional representations -has on the relationship between generalization and identification, and in turn how this impacts performance when multiple items must be processed at once (i.e., processing capacity).

The focus of RDT (Shannon, 1959) is on the relationship between the compression of representations (i.e., the reduction in their complexity) and the accuracy of information transmission that those representations support.
text.formatted: The focus of RDT <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">(Shannon, 1959)</ref> is on the relationship between the compression of representations (i.e., the reduction in their complexity) and the accuracy of information transmission that those representations support.

text.text: Compression can be quantified in terms of the mutual information between a signal presented to the system and its encoding (i.e., the representation of that signal).
Accuracy is quantified in terms of a distortion function, that defines a loss with respect to some task.

The task can be as simple as conveying the signal itself or, more generally, as a mapping from a set of possible signals to corresponding responses, and distortion is quantified by some measure of mismatch between each signal and the task-relevant response for that signal given its representation.

If there is any redundancy among representations (i.e., more than one representation for a given signal), then compression can be lossless (i.e., achieved without any distortion, or loss of accuracy).
This was the focus of early work on efficient coding in neuroscience and cognition (Barlow, 1961).
text.formatted: This was the focus of early work on efficient coding in neuroscience and cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Barlow, 1961)</ref>.

text.text: Absent such redundancy, then compression leads to distortion.

Where there is distortion, it can be mitigated by increasing the complexity of the representations, allowing them to carry more information and thus more accurately map each signal to its task-relevant response.
However, more complex codes require higher transmission rates, since more information must be transmitted per signal.

RDT provides a formal framework for capturing this tradeoff, and the optimization of this tradeoff defines a Pareto front that describes the maximum accuracy that can be expected for a given distortion function and level of representational complexity (or, conversely, the minimum distortion achievable for a given level of compression; see vertical plane of Figure 2).
text.formatted: RDT provides a formal framework for capturing this tradeoff, and the optimization of this tradeoff defines a Pareto front that describes the maximum accuracy that can be expected for a given distortion function and level of representational complexity (or, conversely, the minimum distortion achievable for a given level of compression; see vertical plane of Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: The IB (Tishby et al., 2000) represents a special case of this problem, in which the distortion function corresponds to the difference in the value of some variable associated with a signal (e.g., the assignment of a category label to some object) and the value of that variable predicted by the encoding of the signal.
text.formatted: The IB <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">(Tishby et al., 2000)</ref> represents a special case of this problem, in which the distortion function corresponds to the difference in the value of some variable associated with a signal (e.g., the assignment of a category label to some object) and the value of that variable predicted by the encoding of the signal.

text.text: Considerable empirical evidence supports the idea that human information processing often approaches the Pareto optimal relationship between compression and accuracy as specified by the IB within the RDT framework (Sims, 2018; Zaslavsky et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Considerable empirical evidence supports the idea that human information processing often approaches the Pareto optimal relationship between compression and accuracy as specified by the IB within the RDT framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">(Sims, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b183">Zaslavsky et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: While RDT, and IB as an example, formalize the tradeoff between accuracy and compression, neither provides a normative account of the extent to which compression should be favored over accuracy when these are in tension (i.e., when there is no redundancy in the representations; though see Shamir et al., 2010, for a treatment of IB for finite samples).
text.formatted: While RDT, and IB as an example, formalize the tradeoff between accuracy and compression, neither provides a normative account of the extent to which compression should be favored over accuracy when these are in tension (i.e., when there is no redundancy in the representations; though see <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">Shamir et al., 2010</ref>, for a treatment of IB for finite samples).

text.text: Under such conditions, compression may nevertheless be viewed as advantageous, or at least worth the cost of distortion, for at least two reasons.
One is that it lessens representational demands, and thus is less physically costly.
This may offset the cost of distortion, or even pose an upper limit on complexity, and thus a lower bound on compression.

This, in turn, impacts distortion and constrains processing capacity, providing a normative account of such constraints.

Some theories have suggested that such costs can explain the upper bound on processing capacity observed in human cognitive functions such as working memory (e.g., Ma et al., 2014; Wilken and Ma, 2004).
text.formatted: Some theories have suggested that such costs can explain the upper bound on processing capacity observed in human cognitive functions such as working memory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Ma et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b180">Wilken and Ma, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Here, however, we focus on compression that reflects another factor: representational structure that supports generalization.
As illustrated above, compositional and semantic representations both involve forms of representational sharing that support generalization, and can be thought of as forms of compression.

In this article, we formalize the effects of such representational structure on generalization (operationalized in terms of similarity judgments), and the consequences these have both for more traditional measures of performance (operationalized as signal identification) and processing capacity (i.e., identification in multi-item settings, that quantifies the number of items that can be represented simultaneously while being kept distinct).

Specifically, we show that under reasonable assumptions and conditions, levels of compression (e.g., imposed by semantically structured representations) that optimize generalization are associated with amounts of distortion that limit identification.

Figure 2 shows the relationship of such optimization of generalization to the traditional Pareto front associated with the RDT, that relates compression to traditional measures of accuracy (i.e., identification).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref> shows the relationship of such optimization of generalization to the traditional Pareto front associated with the RDT, that relates compression to traditional measures of accuracy (i.e., identification).

text.text: Critically, we show that such constraints in identification have dire consequences for processing capacity (i.e., identification in multi-item settings), limiting this to the range observed by Miller.
We refer to this relationship between generalization and processing capacity as the Miller-Shepard Law.
Below, we provide the foundations for our operationalization of generalization, grounded on classic work in cognitive science.
Understanding the relationship between representation and generalization is one of the most fundamental and longstanding goals in cognitive science.
Perhaps the most definitive and influential treatment of this is Shepard's (1987) Universal Law of Generalization.
text.formatted: Perhaps the most definitive and influential treatment of this is <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Shepard's (1987)</ref> Universal Law of Generalization.

text.text: This asserts that information should be represented in a form that is monotonically related to similarity structure in the world that is relevant to how the agent should respond to such information.

Importantly, this allows the specific metric properties of internal ("psychological") representations to vary from those of the physical world, so long as they capture the same similarity structure; such metricity is generally referred to as semanticity.

Specifically, the law asserts that "the probability that a response. . . to any stimulus will generalize to any other is an invariant monotonic function of the [psychological] distance between them. .. [and] to a good approximation, this probability of generalization decays exponentially with this distance" (Shepard, 1987; p.1317).
text.formatted: Specifically, the law asserts that "the probability that a response. . . to any stimulus will generalize to any other is an invariant monotonic function of the [psychological] distance between them. .. <ref type="bibr">[and]</ref> to a good approximation, this probability of generalization decays exponentially with this distance" <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">(Shepard, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr">p.1317)</ref>.

text.text: Based on these principles, Shepard was able to derive psychological metric spaces (i.e., of internal representations) that could predict with remarkable accuracy empirical data concerning human psychophysical judgments, all of which exhibited strikingly reliable exponential gradients of generalization.

Intuitively, the generalization gradient can be thought of as reflecting a form of representational sharing, in the sense that representations overlap to the extent that they lead to similar responses, while dissimilar representations are more distinct, or separated.
From an information-theoretic perspective, the generalization gradient implements a form of compression that supports generalization, and aligns with human psychophysical judgments.

Sims (2018) used RDT to derive the optimality of the exponential generalization gradient as a form of compression, providing a normative, information-theoretic underpinning for Shepard's Universal Law of Generalization.
Crucially, however, both RDT and Shepard take the width of the generalization gradient to be determined by a free parameter.

In the next section, after introducing Sims' RDT approach, we show that an optimal value of the parameter can be derived as a solution to maximizing performance in a generalization task, and that adopting that optimal generalization gradient (equivalently, adopting that amount of compression) leads to severe capacity limits.

Critically, observe that the RDT β parameter controlling how much compression should be favored over distortion (or accuracy), also controls the width of the generalization gradient (and hence the behavioral overlap between distinct stimulus representations).

Further, we note that many distortion measures D (e.g., those based on distance such as Euclidean ∥x -x∥ 2 ) are symmetric and centered by definition, in which case the generalization gradient simplifies to g(x, x) = exp(-βD(x, x)).
As noted earlier, the RDT formulation is agnostic to the choice of distortion measure.

To examine the distortion that arises when there is semantic (e.g., categorical) structure, we apply Sims' analysis to the case of the problem, analogous to the IB, that takes a particular (categorical) form of structure into account.

The IB problem assumes that stimuli X are associated with some additional relevant variable Y (e.g., a semantic category) via a joint distribution of the form p(x, y) = p(x|y)p(y) (intuitively, this corresponds to a generative process in which a category y is sampled from the prior p(y) and then an instance of that category x is sampled from the conditional p(x|y)).

The goal of the IB problem is to find an optimal encoder p(x|x) that minimizes mutual information I(X; X) (i.e., maximizes compression) while also maximizing the mutual information between the encoded and relevant variables I( X; Y ) (i.e., maximizes accuracy).

In the section below, we provide a simple, abstract operationalization of generalization from which optimal gradients may be derived.

More specifically, we show that if generalization is operationalized in terms of relative similarity judgments, and such judgments arise from decisions subject to virtually any uncertainty, then a gradient can be identified that optimizes generalization performance.
Intuitively, one might expect that there should be a "sweet spot" for the generalization gradient.

This can be seen in the limits: at one extreme, eliminating the generalization gradient (and therefore any compression) effectively renders all representations equally separated from one another (e.g., orthogonal "one hot" codes), precluding the use of similarity for generalization.
At the other extreme, if the gradient is too broad, or flat (maximum compression), then all representations overlap entirely with one another, so that no distinctions are possible.
Thus, generalization should be best served by some intermediate width of the gradient.

Here, we address this quantitatively, by examining the impact that width of the gradient (i.e., rate or decay of the exponential) has on performance on a simple similarity judgment task that we use to operationalize generalization.

Somewhat counterintuitively, we find that as long as the generalization gradient has a finite decay rate and is continuous, and there is no uncertainty in the decision process, then performance on the generalization task is monotonically improved by narrowing the generalization gradient (see dashed line in Figure 3A below), and performance is best for the narrowest possible gradient (i.e., infinitely small compression).
text.formatted: Somewhat counterintuitively, we find that as long as the generalization gradient has a finite decay rate and is continuous, and there is no uncertainty in the decision process, then performance on the generalization task is monotonically improved by narrowing the generalization gradient (see dashed line in Figure <ref type="figure">3A</ref> below), and performance is best for the narrowest possible gradient (i.e., infinitely small compression).

text.text: However, introducing any amount of noise into the decision process induces a non-monotonicity, that captures the intuition above, with a well-defined optimal width of the gradient.

We demonstrate these effects below, and characterize their relationship to accuracy of performance on an identification task, and their relationship to set size, that undergirds the Miller-Shepard Law.
Identification and generalization tasks.
We begin by examining how the decay rate of the exponential generalization gradient impacts performance in an identification and a generalization task, and how this interacts with set size.

The former replicates the structure of tasks commonly used to assess limits in processing capacity (e.g., Luck and Vogel, 1997; Miller, 1956); we use the latter to assess generalization under conditions as similar to the identification task as possible.
text.formatted: The former replicates the structure of tasks commonly used to assess limits in processing capacity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Luck and Vogel, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Miller, 1956)</ref>; we use the latter to assess generalization under conditions as similar to the identification task as possible.

text.text: Both tasks have the same basic structure: an agent is presented with and required to represent a set S of N stimuli that are drawn from a superset of task-relevant stimuli; the agent is then required to select an item from S based on a probe and a prompt.
In the identification task, the probe is drawn from S, and the agent is prompted to select the item in S to which it is identical.
Again, this is the design commonly used to assess capacity limits, by varying the set size N .

Critically, in the generalization task, the probe is specifically chosen to not be in S, and the agent is prompted to select the item that is most similar to the probe (and hence its properties are most likely to generalize to the probe; Shepard, 1987).

The foregoing analysis indicates that accuracy of both identification and generalization are optimized by using the narrowest gradient -i.e., least compressed (or most separated) representations -possible.

However, as noted earlier, it is commonly assumed that less compression -i.e., greater complexity -is costly in terms of representational resources (e.g., code length or precision), and that this may sometimes favor compression at the expense of accuracy. Zaslavsky et al., 2018 provided evidence of this within the context of the IB formulation for the domain of color naming; and Sims, 2016 provided evidence of a similar effect in perceptual judgment and working memory tasks similar to those addressed by Miller (1956), suggesting that empirically observed generalization gradients (which, in contrast to the analysis above, are not minimal) may reflect capacity constraints in representation (that is, physical limits to representational complexity).

text.text: Below we introduce another possibility.
Decision uncertainty and non-monotonicity of generalization performance.

The analysis described above assumes that the encoding, representation, and decoding of information -and any computations based on these -are free of any noise in the decision process, and that any constraints on performance (i.e., distortion) are attributable to the representations themselves (i.e., compression).

However, surprisingly and significantly, adding noise to the decoding process itself qualitatively alters the effect of β on generalization error; specifically, it induces a non-monotonic relationship between com-pression and generalization, comporting with the intuition suggested above (and by others; e.g., Shamir et al., 2010; Sims, 2016), that there is an intermediate amount of compression that optimizes generalization (implemented here as the exponential decay rate β).

text.text: Finally, we consider the extent to which reducing decision noise ∆ relaxes the constraint on generalization performance, and thus the impact that optimizing for generalization has on identification performance.
The exact formula for β * as a function of ∆ (β * (∆) is, again, not analytically tractable.

Appendix A.3 provides further analytic insight into why the severe processing capacity constraint persists even as decision noise is significantly reduced.

In particular, Equation (A22) characterizes the dependence of maximum information in the identification task on decision noise level, mediated through the selection of the generalization gradient that is optimal for the generalization task.

The equation reveals that dependence to be doubly logarithmic: the optimal generalization gradient is logarithmic in decision noise, and the maximal information in the identification task is logarithmic in the generalization gradient.

In summary, these analyses show that decreasing noise has a relatively weak impact on raising β * and I * i , and thus on ameliorating the impact that optimizing for generalization has in limiting identification accuracy.

In aggregate, the results in this section show that any noise in the decision process induces non-monotonicity in the relationship between the generalization gradient and generalization performance, with an optimum in the former that maximizes the latter.

Furthermore, the analyses reveal that even for vanishingly small amounts of noise, optimizing for generalization is associated with dramatic decreases in identification accuracy that, in turn, is greatly amplified as set size increases. Sims (2018) noted that "adaptive behavior requires perceptual generalization and discrimination abilities that are finely calibrated to the costs of perceptual error" (p. 652).

text.text: Here, we show that, assuming there is any uncertainty in the decision process, then such calibration must face the draconian effect that optimizing for generalization has on reducing identification accuracy, and the effect that this has on reducing processing capacity as the size of the set of items that must be discriminated increases.

This is consistent with the evidence that people favor generalization in tasks that require it, despite the constraints on processing capacity that this imposes -tasks such as those considered by Miller, and that we consider in more detail with a neural network model below (see Section 4).
Finally, we note that the analyses above were restricted to a generalization gradient (i.e., semanticity) as the form of compression, involving features that varied along a single dimension.

They did not take account of compositionality, another form of structure that uses compression for generalization, but assumes that items can be represented by features that vary along more than one dimension.
Compositionality is commonly exploited in experimental tasks used to study processing constraints, and thus we extend our treatment to address this in the sections that follow.
The foregoing analyses focus on an exponential generalization gradient -consistent with Shepard's Universal Law of Generalization -as a form of compression.
This represents a form of semanticity, in which representations are organized in a metric space.
However, as discussed earlier in the Illustrative Example, compositionality is another form of structure that is also commonly considered to be important for learning and generalization.

One way to think about the relationship between these is as different forms of covariance structure, or representational sharing (see Figure 7): Semanticity reflects covariance (sharing) among the features within a given dimension (e.g., the representations of red and pink are more highly correlated than red and blue); while compositionality reflects the absence of covariation among features across dimensions (e.g., colors are not correlated with positions).

In Appendix, Section E.1, we offer more detailed definitions of semanticity and compositionality, and how these relate to assumptions about structure in the world.

Compositionality demands representations with multiple dimensions, which in turn introduces factorial complexity into the integrals that must be calculated for the formal analyses developed in the previous section, making them intractable.

We extended the abstract model above in three ways.
(1) We committed to a gridlike code -a well-known similarity-preserving code in biological systems -and show that the same pattern of effects holds in this setting.

(2) The results also show that the need to transiently bind separate features from otherwise independent dimensions, imposed by compositional representations, can induce uncertainty (via superposition) that, when operating over correlated grid-like codes, is sufficient to create a tradeoff without any external decision noise.
(3) We evaluated the generalization/identification tradeoff when the decision process is determined by the iterative dynamics of a Hopfied-Ising model, rather than a static argmax decision rule.
We begin by providing an analysis of these factors in the model, relating these to the formal analysis presented in the first part of this paper.
We then show that when the model is used to simulate the tasks considered by Miller 1956, it reproduces the empirical observations that were the focus of his inquiry.

text.text: This specific choice of codes was motivated by both theoretical and empirical considerations.

Theoretically, prior work has shown that grid codes exemplify representational efficiency (Chandra et al., 2023; Fiete et al., 2008; Stachenfeld et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2015), minimizing the number of variables necessary to cover the space (Wei et al., 2015) while promoting generalization (Frankland et al., 2019; Mondal et al., 2023; Whittington et al., 2020).

text.text: This matrix serves both as the representation of what was where and as the weight matrix for retrieval.
The N patterns are superimposed in the same L × L matrix, where each pattern contributes ξ i (ξ i ) ⊤ .
We assume that probing with ξ p produces a single Ldimensional vector h = W ξ p .
Identification requires discriminating which of N stored patterns this vector matches most closely.
Although the code space contains 2 L possible binary patterns, a single-probe linear readout can only resolve ≤∼ L at one time.
Moreover, metric codes are necessarily correlated-nearby stimuli must have similar codes for effective generalization -and so the patterns partially interfere.
If the patterns were orthogonal, each pattern would write to a non-overlapping subspace of W .
But with correlated patterns these sub-spaces overlap meaningfully.
When patterns are correlated, Figure 10 column three shows that superposition alone is sufficient to limit identification ability without further decision noise.

text.text: Finally, we consider yet another potential source of uncertainty in the neural network model, that arises as a consequence of retrieval dynamics and thus, analogous to ∆, is intrinsic to the decision process itself.
Specifically, when the settling process of the recurrent network: is applied asynchronously until convergence, it becomes sensitive to the correlational structure of the stored patterns.
Unlike retrieval via selection of the stored item most similar to h, here, an early bit flip toward a neighboring attractor may continue in that direction with each update.
Correlated patterns-optimized for generalization-have overlapping attractor basins, so it is possible for the dynamics to settle to a neighboring pattern rather than the target.
This has direct consequences for processing capacity.

When the patterns in a memory set are uncorrelated, increasing the number of nodes in a simple auto-associative memory increases the the number of distinct associations (i.e., bindings) that the system can distinctly represent at the same time at the classic rate, given by: L 2 log 2 L (McEliece et al., 1987) or the frequently-cited approximate 0.138L (Hopfield, 1982).

text.text: However, even relatively small correlations (e.g., r ∼ 0.01) dramatically limit this increase, which in turn limits processing capacity in settings that rely on such bindings to associate the features belonging to each individual item in a display.

As in the abstract model, processing capacity is heavily constrained by the amount of correlational structure in the representations, with even modest increases in correlation dramatically restricting capacity.

text.text: To summarize, in this section, we have extended the abstract model to incorporate plausible similarity-preserving codes and sources of processing uncertainty in biological systems, showing that: (1) the trade-off between generalization and identification derived for the abstract model above emerges naturally from variation of grid-coding scaling; (2) the binding mechanism itself introduces uncertainty in readout, distinct from the independent and additive decision noise of the abstract model, but with a similar effect; and (3) the retrieval dynamics of an autoassociative memory induce an effect similar to decision noise (∆) used in the abstract model, that leads to even more aggressive limits in processing capacity.

In the next section we use these commitments to directly simulate behavioral performance in the tasks considered by Miller (1956), comprised of embedding, binding, memory, and response processes (Figure 12).

text.text: Processing Capacity: the MEME Model.

As outlined above, we adopt two core assumptions to model performance: (1) grid-like compositional codes bound through Hebbian association; and (2) the inferential dynamics of autoassociative memory for retrieval.

In the model, grid cells project to a memory buffer W (Equation ( 16)) implemented as a simple recurrent neural network Hopfield, 1982, with nodes corresponding to coding elements in the embedding layer (e.g., grid cells).
text.formatted: In the model, grid cells project to a memory buffer W (Equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_23">16</ref>)) implemented as a simple recurrent neural network <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Hopfield, 1982</ref>, with nodes corresponding to coding elements in the embedding layer (e.g., grid cells).

text.text: Each item in a display is defined by a combination of feature values along several dimensions (such as color and spatial location), so that every possible item can be represented compositionally as a unique pattern of activity z(x) over the nodes of the network.

For a given context c (e.g., a trial of a task), conjunctive representations are formed by binding the codes for each item's task-relevant feature values, together with the current context and corresponding response, through rapid Hebbian weight updates that are specific to and reset for each new context.
12,13   The Hebbian weight update minimizes an energy function over the nodes corresponding to the feature values of each item and its context (Figure 1B).
text.formatted: 12,13   The Hebbian weight update minimizes an energy function over the nodes corresponding to the feature values of each item and its context (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>).

text.text: Hebb's rule achieves this by capturing how feature values vary and co-vary in the observed data, yielding the maximum entropy estimate of the statistics over z(x c ) while minimizing the energy of each representation Amit, 1989; MacKay, 1991.
text.formatted: Hebb's rule achieves this by capturing how feature values vary and co-vary in the observed data, yielding the maximum entropy estimate of the statistics over z(x c ) while minimizing the energy of each representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Amit, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">MacKay, 1991</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, we refer to this as the MEME model.

In information-theoretic terms, the embedding layer and associative memory con- 12 Here we focus on Hebbian learning for rapid associative binding through weight modifications (i.e., in "weight space").

In the Appendix (Section C.3), we show that similar effects obtain when tensor product representations Smolensky, 1990 are used to bind representations as unique activity patterns (i.e., in "state space"), which may reflect working memory rather than episodic memory as the store, highlighting the generality of the principles involved.

text.text: 13 This differs from the standard use of Hebbian learning in models of episodic memory (e.g., K. A. Norman  stitute a processing channel for encoding information about the display and task demand and transmitting it to the selected response.

A context c constitutes a single use of this channel-whether a single trial (as in working memory tasks) or a block of trials within an experimental condition (as in the perceptual judgment and numerical estimation tasks considered below).
We evaluate the capacity of this channel by quantifying how many items can be stored simultaneously while maintaining their identity.

Note that while the compositional codes used to represent feature values develop over a long timescale, the Hebbian bindings that form conjunctive representations operate on the timescale of experimental variation-within a specific context-and are specific to that context.
Finally, variability in memory retrieval dynamics in the autoassociative network serves as the mechanistic analog of the decision noise assumed in the formal simulations above.
We applied the model outlined above to the three tasks highlighted by Miller (1956): immediate (or "working") memory; absolute perceptual identification; and numerosity judg-ment.
text.formatted: We applied the model outlined above to the three tasks highlighted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Miller (1956)</ref>: immediate (or "working") memory; absolute perceptual identification; and numerosity judg-ment.

text.text: Though these three tasks operate over different time scales and different domains of information, in each the task-relevant input-output mappings (x c → y c ) require mediation by conjunctive codes (z c ) that, we assume, were not already present in the system's existing set of codes (i.e., they involved novel or unfamiliar pairings of features across dimensions).
They must therefore be constructed compositionally, as combinations of existing codes along each dimension, such as of colors and locations or reference tones and their corresponding labels.

For each task, we constructed a network with sufficient representational "expressivity" to uniquely encode any pair of feature values an agent might need to distinguish, along each dimension, in that task.

We formally quantify expressivity as the joint entropy of the collection of nodes in the network (H(z 1 , . . . , z L )) when feature values at sampled at random along each dimension (See Appendix C.2 for details).

For example, if we assume an agent can distinguish the location of any pair of N equally probable points in a 2D spatial array, we would require a representational scheme with a joint entropy of k = log 2 N bits of information.

Although the most efficient codes for doing so would be random vectors assigned to each code in network with L nodes, where L = k, (as in the classic analyses of auto-associative networks), such codes would fail to support generalization, given that they are not similarity-preserving.

Instead, to implement similarity structure, guided by the properties of grid-like coding described above as well as empirical psychophysical data, we implemented a coding scheme that provided the desired joint entropy of ∼ k bits for each dimension.
In practice, this means that L > k.
text.formatted: In practice, this means that L > k.

text.text: For example, for a 2D spatial display of 9.8° × 7.3°, as in Luck and Vogel (1997), we use published work on Vernier acuity (Frisén and Frisén, 1981; Westheimer and Beard, 1998) and estimates that agents could likely distinguish approximately 715,400 spatial locations (see Appendix C.2 for additional details).
text.formatted: For example, for a 2D spatial display of 9.8° × 7.3°, as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Luck and Vogel (1997)</ref>, we use published work on Vernier acuity <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Frisén and Frisén, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b178">Westheimer and Beard, 1998)</ref> and estimates that agents could likely distinguish approximately 715,400 spatial locations (see Appendix C.2 for additional details).

text.text: If each of these spatial locations is equiprobable, an observation that a stimulus is located at a particular spatial position would carry 19.47 bits of information.
We therefore seek a grid-like coding scheme that scales 8 frequencies at √ e and has a representational capacity of ∼19.47 bits.

We find that a binarized grid-code with 32 nodes (8 frequencies x 4 phases) has a joint entropy of ∼19.5 bits and an average between-pattern Pearson correlation of r ∼ 0.14, and use such a code to represent spatial position in our simulations.
We use a similar reasoning procedure to derive grid-codes for other dimensions (e.g., color, number, pitch).

Although these are estimates and vary from dimension to dimension, we note a few general points about the model before describing specific results: First, joint entropy of 10-20 often appears sufficient to represent each dimension-specific distinction agents can make.

Although this quantity gets larger for high dimensional semantic representations, it is worth noting that a code with a joint entropy of 265 bits would permit the unique identification of each atom in the universe (assuming 10 80 atoms) -this means that systems with even seemingly modest joint entropies have considerable representational capacity.

Second, in this formalism, as semantic precision increases (higher joint entropy, narrower generalization gradient β), so does expected working memory capacity, as has been observed empirically (Alvarez and Cavanagh, 2004; Brady and Störmer, 2022).
text.formatted: Second, in this formalism, as semantic precision increases (higher joint entropy, narrower generalization gradient β), so does expected working memory capacity, as has been observed empirically <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alvarez and Cavanagh, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Brady and Störmer, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Third, and most critically, as shown above, with even small amounts of correlational structure in the code, processing capacity is expected to remain strikingly low, near Miller's magical number.
Here we provide a brief summary of the empirical findings, and our models' account of them.

Nevertheless, we assumed it required the same form of structured (i.e,. generalizable) codes and binding mechanisms to represent the arbitrary (i.e., novel) pairing of the number of items and their positions used in the task.

Accordingly, the model's representation of the display was generated as follows: For each of the N items in the display, item i ∈ {1, . . . , N } was selected randomly without replacement from the set of remaining Ni items, the code for its position was added to the sum of the codes for the preceding Ni items, that sum was paired with the code for the number i, and the pair was stored (bound) in the weights of the associative memory.

This provided the model with a set of numerosity representations for the display, each of which was the conjunction of a number code with a representation of the simultaneously embedded positions for the corresponding number of items.

The model was tested by encoding the display as described above, then presenting it as input and allowing the network's activity state to settle, and finally taking the representation of the number code with the shortest distance to the settled state as the network's response regarding the number of items in the display (Figure 15B).

The constraints on perceptual processing and immediate memory capacity, famously referred to by Miller (1956) as the "magical number 7," have largely remained a mystery.
text.formatted: The constraints on perceptual processing and immediate memory capacity, famously referred to by <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Miller (1956)</ref> as the "magical number 7," have largely remained a mystery.

text.text: This might be considered even more perplexing, given that similar constraints seem to extend beyond tasks involving perception and memory, to ones involving other functions that have been equally foundational in the study of cognition and the brain, including attention, multitasking capability and cognitive control (Posner and Snyder, 1975; Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977; Treisman and Gelade, 1980).
text.formatted: This might be considered even more perplexing, given that similar constraints seem to extend beyond tasks involving perception and memory, to ones involving other functions that have been equally foundational in the study of cognition and the brain, including attention, multitasking capability and cognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">(Posner and Snyder, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">Treisman and Gelade, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we have identified a potential source of these constraints from an information-theoretic perspective, in terms of a fundamental tradeoff between the value of compression, in the form of structured representational sharing that affords generalization, and the constraints that this imposes on processing capacity -the ability to accurately distinguish those representations when processed at the same time.

We have shown that, in the presence of any decision noise: a) even modest amounts of compression, that support generalization, dramatically restrict processing capacity; b) this is observed for psychophysically and neurally informed types of representational structure and processing mechanisms; and c) this account can provide a unified, normative explanation of the restrictive constraints on performance observed across the range of tasks that puzzled Miller (1956).

text.text: In the remainder of this article we consider several questions raised by this account: i) How does it relate to the information-theoretic treatment of capacity limits presented in Miller's paper?
ii) How does it relate to previous applications of information theory to learning and representation in cognitive science and neuroscience?
iii) How does it relate to prominent accounts of capacity constraints in working memory and attention?

iv) How do the mechanisms for transient binding postulated by, and central to our models relate to standard psychological and neural mechanisms thought to be responsible for the rapid formation of arbitrary associations?
v) To what extent can our account explain similar capacity constraints in other cognitive capabilities, such as multitasking and cognitive control?
vi) How can these constraints be overcome?
vii) How do our observations relate to seemingly similar issues in statistics, machine learning, and the use of neural network architectures in artificial intelligence?

Miller (1956) article was perhaps the most influential one to call attention to the severe limits on immediate memory (now referred to more commonly as short-term or working memory), that he indelibly imprinted in most people's minds as the magic number 7.
