text.text: Oddly, it is known mostly for that observation alone -though he assiduously referred to those who originally made it (Hayes, 1952; Pollack, 1953) -rather than for the observation that consumed him, and actually motivated him to refer to the number as magical: the diversity of settings and forms in which the same constraint appears.
text.formatted: Oddly, it is known mostly for that observation alone -though he assiduously referred to those who originally made it <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Hayes, 1952;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Pollack, 1953)</ref> -rather than for the observation that consumed him, and actually motivated him to refer to the number as magical: the diversity of settings and forms in which the same constraint appears.

text.text: This led him to surmise "that there may be something deep and profound behind all these sevens, something that is calling out for us to discover it."

Miller was inspired by the initial surge in applications of information theory to perception and memory following Shannon's seminal 1948 paper, and intrigued by the prospect of using information-theoretic measures to solve the mystery of "all the sevens."
In his effort to solve the mystery, Miller focused on a set of tasks that had been used to assess the channel capacity of human cognition as an information transmission system.
Accordingly, he sought to quantify the capacity of memory and perceptual identification in these tasks in terms of the amount of information transferred, measured in bits.

He accepted this as a reasonable measure of capacity for perceptual processing (i.e., performance in the absolute identification and numerosity tasks), but ran into trouble when applying it to immediate memory.
There, he noted that the number of bits transmitted seemed to vary widely depending on the items to be remembered.

For example, decimal digits carry about 3.3 bits each, so remembering seven digits (e.g., a birth date) actually amounts to storing 23 bits of information; and English words carry about ten bits, so remembering seven English words amounts to storing about 70 bits, and so on.

This led Miller to conclude that the constraint on immediate memory is not the absolute amount of information conveyed by the memories, but rather the number of familiar items that must be remembered, which he referred to as "chunks."

Without a similar construct for perception, and without a formal characterization of a chunk, he expressed suspicion that the constraint of 2.5 bits for perception and the seven chunks for immediate memory was "only a pernicious, Pythagorean coincidence."

The work we present here suggests that the disparities Miller observed across tasks may be understood, at least in part, by taking account of representational sharing that reflects correlations among the features of items.

Much like Mathy and Feldman (2012) and Nassar et al. (2018), we suggest that such correlations provide a formal grounding for what Miller referred to as a "chunk" (and that we refer to as an "item"): a pattern of covariation over a set of feature values along one set of dimensions (e.g., color and shape) that is shared over a range of values along other dimensions (e.g., spatial or temporal; see Appendix, Section E.1).

(2018)</ref>, we suggest that such correlations provide a formal grounding for what Miller referred to as a "chunk" (and that we refer to as an "item"): a pattern of covariation over a set of feature values along one set of dimensions (e.g., color and shape) that is shared over a range of values along other dimensions (e.g., spatial or temporal; see Appendix, Section E.1).

text.text: This embraces objects in a display (such as in Figure 1A), but also the digits of a birthday, or the letters of a word.

text.text: Crucially, we show that the pervasiveness of the ∼2.5 bit constraint can be explained by taking account of how representational structure affects identification error, and how this interacts with the number of items that can be distinguishably represented at the same time.

From this perspective, Miller's chunks can be viewed as conjunctive codes (separated representations) dedicated to particular items, that have been acquired through repeated exposure to the correlations among feature values that define those items.

While such codes are not representationally efficient (in information-theoretic terms, they have high complexity), the lack of correlations among them increases their distinctiveness, allowing them to be used at the same time without risk of interference (identification errors), and thus increases the number of items that can be processed at the same time -i.e., they afford higher processing capacity.

Conversely, when such conjunctive codes dedicated to individual items are not available -that is, when the items must be represented as combinations of feature values for which the correlations have not previously been experienced,or at least learned -then compositional codes (a form of representational sharing) must be used that support generalization.
However, the structure of such codes is a form of compression, associated with distortion (identification errors) that limits processing capacity.
These are exactly the conditions imposed by the tasks on which Miller focused.

Furthermore, the formal analyses and simulations we presented indicate that these conditions are subject to a remarkably consistent constraint of approximately ∼2.5 bits of processing capacity, and that this can be traced to a strikingly strong asymmetry in the effects of representational structure (i.e. compression) in the service of generalization, versus processing capacity: Even the modest amounts of representational sharing required to promote generalization have draconian effects on processing capacity.

In sum, inspired by Miller's information-theoretic approach, and his observations of a provocative similarity in processing constraints among tasks that probed perception and memory, we arrive at a conclusion that differs from his, but one that we suspect he may have appreciated: The similarity in constraints does indeed reflect "something deep and profound behind all these sevens:" a relationship between representation and processing in which compression in the service of generalization comes at a disproportionate cost to processing capacity.
This defines an envelope of performance within which any information processing system must operate, that we have dubbed as the Miller-Shepard Law.

We have shown that, with even a modest premium placed on generalization, processing capacity is constrained -in the number of independent items that can be processed at once -to the number that so intrigued Miller.

However, if it is truly a general principle, it should apply not only to the particular phenomena that intrigued Miller but, more broadly, to the wealth of related data and models that have accrued in the nearly seven decades since his landmark article.
In the remainder of this Discussion, we consider some of these connections.
At least two other influential accounts have been taken to explain capacity constraints in working memory and attention.
One attributes the limit to the fixed capacity of a central attentional store, while the other attributes it to a finite resource that must be divided among the items held.
Here we consider how our account relates to each.
14   Fixed central processing capacity.
Perhaps the most commonly proposed source of capacity constraints is a fixed, limited capacity central processing mechanism.

These attribute processing capacity limits to a fixed architectural constraint -for example, some central processing mechanism that only allows one process to be executed at a time 14 Oberauer et al. (2018) have compiled a set of benchmark findings for working memory models.

We note that the present framework engages several of these directly -set-size effects, similarity effects among memoranda, and cross-domain interference; however, it does not yet address findings from other paradigms, such as serial-position and time-based benchmarks -effects that remain an important direction for future research.

akin to the central processing unit of a traditional computer (Pashler, 1994; Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977) or a capacity-limited central, domain-general attentional store with only a small number of slots (Cowan, 2001 (Cowan, , 2015)).

text.text: In contrast to such a fixed architectural constraint, we argue that limits to processing capacity arise from the representational structure demanded by generalization: codes optimized to generalize are necessarily correlated, correlated codes interfere when they must be kept distinct, and this limits the number of such codes that can be processed at the same time.

Critically, the tasks most commonly used to assess attentional and/or working memory capacity use novel or unfamiliar stimuli (e.g., arbitrary combinations of features such as position, color, shape, and/or time of occurrence), precisely in order to probe the flexibility of processing for which attention and working memory are thought to be responsible.
In other words, by design, they involve stimuli that require the use of generalizable representations.
By our account, it is precisely this requirement that imposes the capacity limit.
This provides a normative account of capacity limits in terms of a fundamental representational tradeoff, rather than a fixed architectural constraint.
At the same time, our account is generally well-aligned with the idea that the limit is closely associated with attentional function.

For example, the associative binding mechanism in the models we used to simulate Miller's tasks -that allowed the system to flexibly represent arbitrary combinations of features -implemented precisely the binding operation assigned to attention by the Feature Integration Theory of attention Treisman and Gelade, 1980.

text.text: What we believe our account adds is a proposed answer to what determines that capacity: the similarity structure of the codes being bound, which is required for generalization, rather than a fixed architectural constraint.

This proposal is also consistent with Miller's principle of chunking, which affords greater capacity through the use of previously-formed associations (e.g., between a word and its constituent letters) to combine elements into distinguishable representations (the word).

In such cases, the capacity constraint is largely determined by the representational level at which the combinations are less familiar (e.g., an arbitrary sequence of word combinations vs. a sentence); at that level, once again, codes are required that afford generalization (e.g., compositional codes that bind each word or letter to a position); however, as we have argued, because such codes are less distinguishable they are subject to capacity constraints.

This view is consistent with observations by Halford et al. (2005 Halford et al. ( , 2007) ) that capacity is limited not by the number of elements held but by the number of relations among them that must be simultaneously represented, with a limit of roughly four variables.

The limit on relational complexity and the limit on set size may be a single constraint on how many codes can be superimposed before interference renders them indistinguishable.

text.text: The authors show that a signal detection model with a single memory-strength parameter -target confusability competition (TCC) -accounts for continuous-report, n-AFC, and change-detection data across set sizes, delays, and encoding times, in tasks closely related to those considered here.
TCC is closely related to our abstract model: in both, a probe elicits a graded similarity signal across candidate items, noise is added, and the maximum is selected.
Critically, in TCC the similarity among response alternatives follows an independently measured exponential function rather than being linear in stimulus space.

TCC takes that function as given, consistent with its derivation from efficient-coding principles (Sims, 2018), and estimates d ′ separately for each condition; the resulting decline of d ′ with set size follows a power law that the authors note is broadly consistent with resource theories, without committing to a mechanism.
text.formatted: TCC takes that function as given, consistent with its derivation from efficient-coding principles <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">(Sims, 2018)</ref>, and estimates d ′ separately for each condition; the resulting decline of d ′ with set size follows a power law that the authors note is broadly consistent with resource theories, without committing to a mechanism.

text.text: Our current work bears on two issues both accounts leave open.
First, what determines the width of the similarity function (and hence processing capacity)?
We show that when the width is optimized for generalization, identification performance is constrained to be low, which in turn limits processing capacity.
Second, what mechanism produces the decline with set size?
Resource theories hold that a fixed pool is shared among N items, so each is represented less precisely.
We attribute this decrease in precision to representational interference: N correlated codes superimposed in a common substrate corrupt one another, so each is retrieved less reliably.

On this view, representational sharing determines the severity of the constraint: optimization for generalization accounts for the strikingly restrictive effects on load beyond what may be attributable to the cost of precision alone.
We take the success of TCC across tasks and memory systems as convergent evidence that similarity structure -not a fixed store -is the primary determinant of capacity.
How the structural constraint interacts with the cost of precision is an important direction for future work.
We began our analysis by reviewing RDT, and then used it as framework within which to formally characterize the relationship between semanticity, as a form of compression, and processing capacity.

Here, we briefly summarize the contributions we believe our analyses make to the use of RDT for studying cognitive function, and potentially interesting future directions in which this could be taken.
In Section A.4 of the Appendix we consider the formal relationship between our analyses and the Information Bottleneck as an instance of RDT).
RDT is concerned with the effects of distortion on the transmission of information.

Distortion -defined in terms of differences between the source and decoded signals -can be due to perturbations of the signal during transmission, usually referred to as noise, or more structured forms of perturbations (e.g., representational) that reduce the complexity of the representations used to encode the data, referred to as compression.
The IB (Tishby et al., 2000) focuses on forms of compression that are imposed by some objective (e.g., classification error).

text.formatted: Accordingly, empirical evidence for compression in human cognitive function (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b183">Zaslavsky et al., 2018)</ref> is usually taken to reflect a capacity constraint, either imposed by a fixed limit on representational complexity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">Sims, 2016)</ref>, or the result of a tradeoff against some physical cost (e.g., metabolic) incurred by precision(i.e., complexity; <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Bays and Husain, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b180">Wilken and Ma, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the underlying analyses all assume that compression is the only source of distortion, and that all other processes are lossless (i.e., noise-free).

The work we present here indicates that if another source of distortion is considered -decision noisethe relationship between compression and generalization is qualitatively changed from being monotonic to non-monotonic, such that: a) an intermediate amount of compression can be identified that is optimal for generalization; b) that optimum is associated with considerable degradation in the ability to accurately identify individual items, and thereby processing capacity (see Figure 2).

text.text: This relationship appears with a remarkably small (virtually any) amount of decision noise.

This interaction between decision noise and compression is a potentially important extension of RDT, offering a normative account of how generalization may drive compression, in addition to considerations of capacity noted above.

Our findings, along with those of Sims (2016), contribute to RDT in another potentially important way: by extending analyses of the effects of compression on the processing of individual signals, to the processing of multiple signals at once -what we have referred to more generally as processing capacity.
text.formatted: Our findings, along with those of <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">Sims (2016)</ref>, contribute to RDT in another potentially important way: by extending analyses of the effects of compression on the processing of individual signals, to the processing of multiple signals at once -what we have referred to more generally as processing capacity.

text.text: Here, we found that, when compression is optimized for generalization, the restrictive effects observed on identification are rapidly amplified as the number of items that must be processed (set size) is increased.
At the least, this has value for applications of RDT to cognitive science and neuroscience, where such capacity constraints are widely observed, such as those that were canonized by Miller.

However, as we discuss further on, these are also likely to be as important to the design of artificial agents that more closely approximate the flexibility and efficiency of human cognitive function.
These contributions suggest potential new lines of work, that may help further refine our understanding of the relationship between compression and generalization.
One is suggested by how we operationalized generalization.
We did so by contrasting a generalization task with an identity task.
Both involved the selection of an item in a test set that best matched a probe.
However, they differed in the nature of the match -identicality or similarity -which was manipulated, across the two tasks, by how the probe was sampled.
In the identity task, it was sampled from the test set itself; that is, "within distribution."

This can be thought of as modeling circumstances in which existing knowledge (the test set) has all the information needed to perform the task (identify the probe), and no generalization is required because the probe was chosen to be in the test set.
In contrast, in the generalization task, the probe was chosen to not be an item in the test test; that is, "out of distribution."

This can be thought of as modeling circumstances in which generalization is required: existing knowledge must be represented in a form that shares as much information as possible with the distribution of possible probes, without actually (exactly) representing any of them.
Sampling the probe from a uniform distribution of items outside the test set demanded the most extreme form of generalization.

Importantly, the two extremes that we used define a continuum, in which the need for generalization grows with the disparity between the distribution of existing representations and that of the items that will be encountered in the future (i.e., from which a "probe" may be drawn).
How the effects we have reported here vary when the need for generalization is varied along this continuum remains an open and interesting question.

This question connects to recent work on variable-rate encoding, in which the rate -and so the achievable precision -differs between representations (Hedayati et al., 2022) and can be adapted to the agent's circumstances (Nagy et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This question connects to recent work on variable-rate encoding, in which the rate -and so the achievable precision -differs between representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Hedayati et al., 2022)</ref> and can be adapted to the agent's circumstances <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Nagy et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Our framework suggests one normative driver of such variation: the differential demand for generalization across circumstances, with greater demand favoring intermediate rates and thus more representational sharing.
Similarly, our analyses assumed a particular, and relatively simple form of loss (or objective) closely related to ones used in previous work (e.g., categorization; Zaslavsky et al., 2018).

text.text: The extent to which our findings extend to other forms of loss, tuned to more complex forms of structure (e.g., sequential and/or as hierarchical) that are characteristic of other domains (e.g., natural and formal languages) remains another open question.
Both of these questions present interesting and potentially important directions for future research.
Finally, it is worth noting that a central tenet of RDT is that, for any given distortion, there is a commensurate increase in the complexity of the code that can compensate for the loss.

For example, as suggested by the Illustrative Example presented at the beginning of this article, this increase in complexity can be achieved by using dedicated conjunctive codes for each combination of features to avoid the loss (i.e., avert the "binding problem") imposed by the use of compositionally compressed codes.

More generally, the tension between generalization and processing capacity is a reflection of this principle, wherein the learning of dedicated (e.g., conjunctive) representations decreases identification error, and thereby increases processing capacity -a consideration that we turn to below (and in greater detail in Section E of the Appendix) as a way of formalizing the effects of consolidation, automatization, and "chunking" noted above.

However, as noted there, these processes take time, and thus cannot contribute meaningfully to the rapid and flexible processing of novel states -i.e., generalization -that are required for the kinds of tasks on which Miller focused.

From the perspective of RDT this suggests that, using identification error as the loss, it should be possible to quantify the increase in representational complexity that would be required to compensate for the distortion introduced by forms of structure that support generalization (such semanticity and compositionality).

Doing so could usefully leverage RDT to analyze and characterize the kinds of representations that improve processing capacity in a given domain; that, in turn, could provide a framework for formalizing our understanding of the processes underlying consolidation, automatization and chunking, that we consider further below.

Our work builds on a longstanding and influential tradition of theoretical work in cognitive science and neuroscience, inspired both by statistical physics and information theory (Barlow, 1961; Friston, 2010; Linsker, 1988) suggesting that the brain implements efficient coding to maximize information preservation, given an agent's resource constraints.
text.formatted: Our work builds on a longstanding and influential tradition of theoretical work in cognitive science and neuroscience, inspired both by statistical physics and information theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Barlow, 1961;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Linsker, 1988)</ref> suggesting that the brain implements efficient coding to maximize information preservation, given an agent's resource constraints.

text.text: Here, we argue that by extending this approach to take account of representational structure -viewed, through the lens of RDT, as a form of compression -can help explain an apparent paradox in human cognitive function: on the one hand, the remarkable range of information over which it can operate, as well as the flexibility it exhibits in responding to novel information; and, on the other, the equally striking constraints in processing capacity it exhibits in some settings.
Most previous work has focused on the former -that is, optimal coding that maximizes the ability of the system to come to accurately represent as much information as efficiently as possible.
Furthermore, it has focused largely on probabilistic structure, wherein optimal coding is achieved by adapting representational complexity (e.g., code length) to the frequency of events.
The objective of such forms of optimization is to minimize identification error -the frequency with which the selected code is not identical to the correct one.

Here, we have pointed out that an equally important goal of learning is to represent the similarity structure of the world, the objective of which is to minimize generalization error -the distance of the selected code from the correct one.
This follows from Shepard (1987) Universal Law of Generalization, and relies on the use of representational sharing and attendant compression.
text.formatted: This follows from <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Shepard (1987)</ref> Universal Law of Generalization, and relies on the use of representational sharing and attendant compression.

text.text: Here, we operationalize generalization error as a form of compression, and thus its tension with the traditional focus on minimizing identification error and, accordingly, the optimization of generalization in tension with the optimization of processing capacity.

We have shown that this tradeoff can explain the conditions under which cognitive function is constrained -viz., when it relies on the use of representational sharing, in the form of semantically and/or compositionally structured codes, to process novel items -and the remarkable severity of these constraints even when the amount of structure introduced to the codes is relatively modest.
Our account is closely related to other influential accounts of generalization and how this relates to constraints on processing, that we consider below.

Importantly, however, while all of these formalize the tension between generalization and the ability to identify individual items and/or discriminate them from others, none of these lines of work -nor, to our knowledge, any others -directly analyze the consequences that this has for the number of items that can be processed at once, that we refer to as processing capacity, and that we propose as a principled account of Miller's (1956) observations.

Here, we formalize this tension: we show how optimizing for generalization can explain the commonly observed severity of capacity constraints.
That said, coupling our observations with the approach taken by Gaussian Process models points to interesting and potentially important directions for future research.

For example, how do factors associated with learning (distribution of samples, learning rate, etc.) impact the extent to which a system converges on optimal generalization gradients, and to what extent is this associated with changes in capacity constraints as would be predicted by our account.

It may also provide theoretical guidance for the analysis of brain imaging data, by providing quantitatively precise predictions about the relationship between patterns of brain activity (e.g., correlation among neural representations) and limits to processing capacity (measured behaviorally).
The ability to rapidly associate (bind) compositional representations to process novel items plays a central role in our account, that we assume is supported by some form of associative memory.

This raises two closely related questions: How do such associative mechanisms relate to traditional cognitive constructs, such as episodic memory (EM) and working memory (WM); and what neural mechanisms might be responsible for these?

Rapid associative binding is a hallmark of EM, widely believed to be supported by the hippocampus (e.g., McClelland et al., 1995), and perhaps other structures such as the cerebellum (Musslick et al., 2023; T. W. Webb et al., 2024).

text.text: The presence of such structure in EM is consistent with its role as a mechanism for rapid associative binding of structured representations, and the costs that this incurs, that are central to our account.

Alternatively, it has been proposed that rapid associative binding may occur among representations actively maintained in WM, whether using similar Hebbian mechanisms (Oberauer et al., 2012), phase coupling among oscillating representations (Hommel, 2004; Jensen and Lisman, 1998; Roux et al., 2012), short-term synaptic potentiation (Jonides et al., 2008), the online formation of tensor product representations (Smolensky, 1990; e.g., see Appendix, Section C.3), or through projection into a high-dimensional space of actively maintainable random representations (Bouchacourt and Buschman, 2019).

text.text: One fundamental difference between EM and WM is the durability of the associations formed among representations: a fundamental feature of EM is that such associations are stable, and remain accessible for considerable periods of time after they are formed (hours to years), a feature that is assumed to reflect their formation through modification of synaptic weights.

In contrast, WM is generally assumed to rely on the transient maintenance of information in activity states: associations formed in WM are inaccessible once the corresponding representations are no longer active, presumably after short periods of time (minutes if not seconds; though see Stokes (2015) for the possibility of "activity-silent working memory").

text.text: Use of mechanisms responsible for EM versus WM for binding should thus make different predictions about the influence of the associations formed on subsequent processing over different temporal intervals -a factor that has received some attention (Beukers et al., 2021), but remains an important direction for future research.

text.text: Language is perhaps the most widely recognized domain in which there is pressure for compositionally structured representations that support generalization (Fodor and Pylyshyn, 1988).

text.text: Therefore, based on our considerations, this should be closely accompanied by extreme limits in capacity when multiple similar representational codes must be processed simultaneously.

Such limits were first pointed out by George Miller and Noam Chomsky (Chomsky and Miller, 1958), who observed that we seem to have striking limits in our ability to process syntactically well-formed sentences that require the maintenance and discrimination of phrases with highly similar structure, such as in self-embedded clauses (e.g., "the mouse the cat the dog bit chased hid").

text.text: Modern accounts suggest that the need to manage long-distance dependencies -syntactic, semantic and referential relations that may stretch across dozens of words or even sentences -requires that linguistic representations be actively maintained in working memory which, coupled with similarity-based interference among those linguistic representations, give rise to the severe capacity limits observed in language processing (Gibson, 1998 (Gibson, , 2000;; Lewis, 1996; Lewis et al., 2006).

text.text: What we add here are analyses that indicate such capacity limits were inevitable given the pressures for generalization in language.

The challenge of reliably handling long-distance dependencies in natural language led directly to the development of architectures such as the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), and large language models (LLMs) based on them.
text.formatted: The challenge of reliably handling long-distance dependencies in natural language led directly to the development of architectures such as the Transformer <ref type="bibr" target="#b172">(Vaswani et al., 2017)</ref>, and large language models (LLMs) based on them.

text.text: Such models provide a useful test of the extent to which the tension between generalization and processing capacity is a general principle.
On the one hand, they have massive numbers of parameters, suggesting that resources for representation and processing should not be a strong source of constraint.

On the other hand, they were designed to handle the online processing of long-distance dependencies, and trained under heavy pressure for generalization, suggesting that they should make use of structured codes.
By our account, these factors should together induce strict constraints on processing of multiple items at the same time, similar to the constraints on processing capacity observed in humans.

Remarkably, there is growing evidence that this is the case, when such models are tested under conditions that elicit such constraints in humans: They have difficulty processing sentences involving self-embeddings (with their attention patterns reflecting this; Ryu and Lewis, 2021), and with tasks requiring the simultaneous processing of multiple items composed of arbitrary combinations of features (Campbell et al., 2024).

text.text: We return to the latter where we consider the relevance of our work to artificial systems in greater detail further below.

Our analyses also align with theories about the trajectory of representational structure over the course of language development, that we return to in the section below, where we discuss how learning interacts with the tradeoff between generalization and processing capacity.
All of that said, language involves forms of structure (e.g., sequential and hierarchical) that are substantially more complex than the ones we have examined in this article.

While it stands to reason that generalization will rely on some form of similarity expressed at those higher levels of structure, and that this will require representational sharing that imposes processing constraints similar to the ones we have examined here, evaluating this remains an important challenge for future work.

In this article we have largely adhered to Miller (1956) focus on capacity constraints in tasks that involve perception and/or memory, constraints that we suggested above may extend to language processing.

text.text: Another domain of cognitive function in which similarly restrictive constraints have been observed is in multitasking capability and the allocation of cognitive control.

Here, the constraints are usually framed in terms of a foundational distinction in cognitive psychology, between automatic and control-dependent modes of processing (Posner and Snyder, 1975; Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977).
text.formatted: Here, the constraints are usually framed in terms of a foundational distinction in cognitive psychology, between automatic and control-dependent modes of processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">(Posner and Snyder, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: Control-dependent processing is characterized as highly flexible and general, but subject to interference and therefore limited to inefficient serial processing.
In contrast, automatic processing is deemed less prone to interference and can support efficient parallel processing, but requires extensive practice to achieve and is more rigidly task-dedicated.

The same distinction -sometimes referred to as "dual process" theory" -has been made in other fields using other terms, such as System 1 and System 2 in behavioral economics (Sloman, 1996), model-free (habitual) and model-based (deliberative) in machine learning and neuroscience (Daw et al., 2005; Doya, 1999; Sutton and Barto, 1998); and in terms of "thinking fast and slow" in the lay literature (Kahneman, 2011).

text.text: The constraints on control-dependent processing have traditionally been attributed to reliance on a centralized, general purpose mechanism that is responsible for the flexibility of human cognitive function, including its ability to respond effectively to novel situations (D. A. Norman and Shallice, 1986), but that is capacity-limited and restricted to the serial execution of processing, akin to the central processing unit (CPU) of a traditional computer (Pashler, 1988; Posner and Snyder, 1975; Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977).
text.formatted: The constraints on control-dependent processing have traditionally been attributed to reliance on a centralized, general purpose mechanism that is responsible for the flexibility of human cognitive function, including its ability to respond effectively to novel situations (D. A. <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Norman and Shallice, 1986)</ref>, but that is capacity-limited and restricted to the serial execution of processing, akin to the central processing unit (CPU) of a traditional computer <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">(Pashler, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Posner and Snyder, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: However, a longstanding alternative -"multiple resources theory" (Allport et al., 1972; Navon and Gopher, 1979) -suggests that processing is distributed, and that constraints arise not from reliance on a "central bottleneck" imposed by a capacity-limited control mechanism, but rather when different processes must compete to use the same set of shared local resources.
text.formatted: However, a longstanding alternative -"multiple resources theory" <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allport et al., 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Navon and Gopher, 1979)</ref> -suggests that processing is distributed, and that constraints arise not from reliance on a "central bottleneck" imposed by a capacity-limited control mechanism, but rather when different processes must compete to use the same set of shared local resources.

text.text: This has received growing support from computational analyses (e.g., Meyer and Kieras, 1997; Musslick et al., 2023), in which "local resources" are sets of representations required to perform a given task.
text.formatted: This has received growing support from computational analyses (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Meyer and Kieras, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Musslick et al., 2023)</ref>, in which "local resources" are sets of representations required to perform a given task.

text.text: In these models, interference arises when different tasks (e.g., naming the color versus shape of a stimulus) rely on a shared set of representations (e.g., phonological codes), but those tasks require different representations within the set that must compete for activation at the same time.

This has lead to a formulation of the distinction between control-dependent versus automatic processing in terms of a tradeoff between, respectively: i) the shared use of compositional representations, that can be acquired efficiently and flexibly reconfigured to perform novel tasks, but subject to interference that poses the demand for serialization of processing imposed by control mechanisms; and ii) the formation of separated, conjunctive representations (of stimuli and associated responses) that are less subject to interference that allows parallel execution (i.e., multitasking) and thus less demand for control, but require time and effort to acquire and are more rigidly task-specific (Musslick et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This has lead to a formulation of the distinction between control-dependent versus automatic processing in terms of a tradeoff between, respectively: i) the shared use of compositional representations, that can be acquired efficiently and flexibly reconfigured to perform novel tasks, but subject to interference that poses the demand for serialization of processing imposed by control mechanisms; and ii) the formation of separated, conjunctive representations (of stimuli and associated responses) that are less subject to interference that allows parallel execution (i.e., multitasking) and thus less demand for control, but require time and effort to acquire and are more rigidly task-specific <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">(Musslick et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This interpretation can be viewed as another expression of the information-theoretic principles we have identified here; viz., the tradeoff between generalization afforded by shared (i.e., compressed) representations, and processing capacity afforded by separated (i.e,. more complex) ones: Control-dependent, serial processing can be viewed as an adap-tation by the cognitive system required to mitigate the potential for interference incurred by representational sharing required for generalization.

From this perspective, the constraints in capacity so intimately associated with control-dependent processing can be viewed as reflecting its purpose" rather than a shortcoming: the imposition of serial processing to avert the risk of interference (i.e., identification errors) incurred by the use of representations that support generalization.
In short, control mechanisms may have co-evolved with the ability to learn shared representations as a condition for their use.

This framing offers a unified account of capacity constraints, that spans perception, working memory, and tasks that rely on cognitive control, that provides a potentially valuable framework future empirical work in these domains.
It also provides a formally rigorous, and potentially normative framework within which to consider how and when such constraints may be overcome, that we turn to next.
Recoding.

While there has been considerable work in cognitive science and neuroscience that focuses on representational learning and its relationship to generalization (Fang and Sims, 2025; Frankland et al., 2019; Franklin and Frank, 2020; T. W. Webb et al., 2021; Whittington et al., 2020), considerably less has focused on its relationship to limitations in processing capacity.
text.formatted: While there has been considerable work in cognitive science and neuroscience that focuses on representational learning and its relationship to generalization <ref type="bibr">(Fang and Sims, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Frankland et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Franklin and Frank, 2020</ref>; T. W. <ref type="bibr" target="#b176">Webb et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b179">Whittington et al., 2020)</ref>, considerably less has focused on its relationship to limitations in processing capacity.

text.text: As we have noted, this relationship is brought into sharp relief by tasks that involve novel or unpredictable stimuli -including those on which Miller focused.

However, as noted just above, there are also many conditions under which people exhibit remarkable processing capacity, evidenced by parallel processing capabilities, from perception (e.g., identifying a face in a crowd) to action (e.g., talking and driving, no less the vast array of vital functions carried out in parallel by the brain outside of awareness).
We assume that this relies on the use of dedicated conjunctive representations that have been acquired over the course of evolution, early in development, or through repeated experience.
Insofar as such representations diminish the likelihood of interference, acquiring and using them is an effective strategy for increasing processing capacity.
Miller referred to this as "chunking" (e.g., representing a string of digits as a single date, or a string of letters as a single word).

Where possible, such recoding (i.e., identifying an existing conjunctive representation that corresponds to its individually presented constituents) is a well known mnemonic device, that can produce dramatic increases in capacity, such as remembering an arbitrary string of 100 digits (Ericsson and Simon, 1980).
text.formatted: Where possible, such recoding (i.e., identifying an existing conjunctive representation that corresponds to its individually presented constituents) is a well known mnemonic device, that can produce dramatic increases in capacity, such as remembering an arbitrary string of 100 digits <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Ericsson and Simon, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Automatization.

Importantly, however, the acquisition of new representations of this sort requires long term learning mechanisms to generate purpose-specific conjunctive codes, by forming enduring associations among existing codes that co-occur with sufficient frequency.
This is what drives the process of automatization that occurs with practice in skill acquisition (Cohen et al., 1990; Logan, 1985; Musslick et al., 2023; Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977).
text.formatted: This is what drives the process of automatization that occurs with practice in skill acquisition <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Cohen et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Logan, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Musslick et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: The framework we have described provides a formally rigorous, normative approach to understanding this canonical trajectory: from capacity-limited, control-dependent performance early in training, that exploits the flexibility of shared representations for generalization, to a more efficient, automatic, parallel form of processing and multitasking capability that comes from the formation of dedicated conjunctive (i.e., separated) representations with time and practice.

It also bears striking parallels to observations and theory regarding representational learning, which is often framed in terms of statistical learning and consolidation, where the same principles may apply.
Consolidation.

Learning patterns of correlation among features has long been used to explain the semantic structure of representations acquired by neural networks (e.g., Hinton, 1986; Rumelhart and Todd, 1993) and, accordingly, as a model of human semantic memory (e.g., Giallanza et al., 2024; McClelland and Rogers, 2003).
text.formatted: Learning patterns of correlation among features has long been used to explain the semantic structure of representations acquired by neural networks (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Hinton, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Rumelhart and Todd, 1993)</ref> and, accordingly, as a model of human semantic memory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Giallanza et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">McClelland and Rogers, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: We assume that such processes, building on and in addition to the process of evolution, give rise to representations with generalization gradients and dimensional structure that support the simple forms of semanticity and compositionality considered in this article.

However, as noted repeatedly, such forms of statistical learning require a relatively slow rate of adaptation to insure that they capture reliable structure in the environment and thus fail, on their own, to explain the rapid forms of adaptation characteristic of human cognition (e.g., McCloskey and Cohen, 1989).
text.formatted: However, as noted repeatedly, such forms of statistical learning require a relatively slow rate of adaptation to insure that they capture reliable structure in the environment and thus fail, on their own, to explain the rapid forms of adaptation characteristic of human cognition (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">McCloskey and Cohen, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) theory was introduced to address this issue, proposing that statistical learning in semantic memory (SM) is complemented by the rapid formation of arbitrary associations in EM (McClelland et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) theory was introduced to address this issue, proposing that statistical learning in semantic memory (SM) is complemented by the rapid formation of arbitrary associations in EM <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(McClelland et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we assume that such functionality supports the binding of (i.e., the rapid formation of associations among) compositionally structured codes, and thus the "online" formation of conjunctive representations required to represent novel objects.
As discussed above, whether this relies on the specific mechanisms of EM proposed by CLS, or others with comparable functionality remains an important and open question.

Importantly, however, CLS also proposes another role for EM: consolidation: the use of associations rapidly formed in EM among previously unassociated representations in SM, to forge new, more stable representations in SM that capture these associations (Kumaran et al., 2016; McClelland et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Importantly, however, CLS also proposes another role for EM: consolidation: the use of associations rapidly formed in EM among previously unassociated representations in SM, to forge new, more stable representations in SM that capture these associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Kumaran et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">McClelland et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: This is assumed to rely on processes such as active rehearsal and/or passive replay that drive statistical learning mechanisms in SM to form these new associations.
Such processes thus support the formation of new, dedicated conjunctive representations corresponding to the ones formed from the binding of compositional representations in EM.

At the same time, this is thought to occur in a manner that preserves as much existing structure as possible (e.g., by sampling representations that have distinct associations in those that are replayed).

Such preservation of existing structure may require narrowing the generalization gradients (i.e., reducing compression) of the newly formed representations with respect to the existing ones that are to be preserved.

In either case -the formation of new, dedicated conjunctive codes, and/or the potential narrowing of generalization gradients -consolidation can be viewed from an informationtheoretic perspective as increasing representational complexity.
From the perspective of this article, it provides a means of increasing processing capacity through the use of dedicated representations that are less subject to interference.

More generally, this suggests that consolidation -the transition over time, and with rehearsal and replay, from flexible but arbitrary associations formed in EM to the richer, domain-specific representations that form semantic knowledge (the representation of meaning and its use in inference) -can be viewed as a process that is homologous to automatization -the transition over time, and with practice, from flexible, control-dependent processing to more efficient, automatic processing that relies on procedural knowledge (skills acquired in the service of action).

Finally, it is also important to note that the use of rapid associative mechanisms for binding of compositional representations -whether for generalization (the primary focus on in this article) or consolation and automatization (as discussed just above) -should be subject to limitations similar to those observed for EM.

For example, while the storage capacity of EM is generally assumed to be extremely large, if not unlimited, the number of independent sets of associations (e.g., among features of an item) that can be either stored or retrieved at the same time is constrained by the same factors of compositionality (the binding problem) and semanticity (proactive interference) as those we have considered in this article.
Relationship to Optimal Coding.

The information-theoretic framework we have described offers a unified, formally rigorous approach to understanding the effects of recoding ("chunking"), as well as the trajectories in representational learning (consolidation) and skill acquisition (automaticity) from flexible forms of processing to more efficient ones, through the formation and use of dedicated, purpose-specific conjunctive representations.
By reducing representational sharing, these reduce the risk of interference, and thus increase processing capacity.

Importantly, the frequency-dependent nature of the learning mechanisms involved accord with a central tenet of optimal coding in RDT: that the complexity of a representation should be reduced with the frequency of its use.
Dedicated conjunctive codes can thereby be viewed as less complex codes (a single representation, rather than the composition of several) for frequently encountered conjunctions.
This has recently been applied to provide a normative account of dual process theory in terms of the minimum description length principle (Moskovitz et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This has recently been applied to provide a normative account of dual process theory in terms of the minimum description length principle <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">(Moskovitz et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we propose that this can be extended beyond the traditional assertion that frequency should impact code length (i.e., complexity), to the idea that frequency should also impact the structure of the codes themselves, and how they relate to one another: new representations should be dedicated to frequently experienced conjunctions of features (i.e., ones that are correlated, comprising specific items) that are not only less complex, but also are less similar to (i.e., share less with and are further from) from those used to support the processing of novel items with which they might be confused.

Note that, while such dedicated conjunctive (i.e., separated) representations may be less complex, as additional (and redundant) representations, they increase the representational complexity of (i.e., the number of representations in) the system as a whole.
This observation warrants two comments.

First, to the extent that such dedicated conjunctive representations can be used compositionally to flexibly represent new, higher level constructs (e.g., individual animals -as dedicated representations of specific conjunctions of features -can be used compositionally to flexibly represent higher-level constructs, such as a circus or a zoo), and thus reflect a form of compression at a higher level of analysis.

Thus, more generally, consolidation and automatization can be viewed as the formation of dedicated representations for high-frequency correlations among representations at lower levels of analysis that can serve one or both of two purposes: i) the separation of those representations from ones with which they might otherwise be confused, to increase processing capacity for their use (akin to "chunking"); and/or ii) their use as elements for compositionally representing higher level novel, or less frequently experienced constructs.

Second, this relationship between frequency-dependent reduction of complexity at one level (in accord with RDT), and its potential to support compression at another level, closely resembles a similar relationship between item versus system level complexity in theories of language development (e.g., Nowak et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Second, this relationship between frequency-dependent reduction of complexity at one level (in accord with RDT), and its potential to support compression at another level, closely resembles a similar relationship between item versus system level complexity in theories of language development (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">Nowak et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: There, it is hypothesized that the system begins, under pressure for expressivity, by developing dedicated representations for high-frequency items (often "irregular" forms; Kirby, 2001).
text.formatted: There, it is hypothesized that the system begins, under pressure for expressivity, by developing dedicated representations for high-frequency items (often "irregular" forms; <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Kirby, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: However, as it is exposed increasingly to structured information (e.g., regular forms), and under the pressure for compression (imposed by the need for communication over limited bandwidth channels), it develops generalizable (e.g., compositional) representations that, while they are more complex (e.g., compared to dedicated conjunctive representations of items), reduce overall system complexity.

Our analyses assumed that such representations had already formed, and focused on the constraints in processing capacity to which they are subject -constraints that are amenable to their use over limited bandwidth channels.

Here, we note that the processes of consolidation and automatization may reflect an additional (perhaps later) phase of acquisition, during which highly frequent and/or useful items, even if they can be represented using generalizable codes, may be assigned simpler codes (again, in accord with RDT), that have the effect of increasing processing capacity.

Interestingly, these phases of acquisition align broadly with observations made about the progression of representations over the course of training in neural networks, including the learning of regular and irregular forms of verb conjugation (Rumelhart and McClelland, 1985), the phenomenon of "grokking" (in which "memorization" is followed by generalization; e.g., Power et al., 2022), and the transition from flexible ("in-context") forms of processing to more efficient, dedicated ("in-weight") forms of processing (e.g., Singh et al., 2023), as well as recent information-theoretic analyses of such learning trajectories of learning (Conklin et al., 2026; Tishby and Zaslavsky, 2015).
text.formatted: Interestingly, these phases of acquisition align broadly with observations made about the progression of representations over the course of training in neural networks, including the learning of regular and irregular forms of verb conjugation <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">(Rumelhart and McClelland, 1985)</ref>, the phenomenon of "grokking" (in which "memorization" is followed by generalization; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">Power et al., 2022)</ref>, and the transition from flexible ("in-context") forms of processing to more efficient, dedicated ("in-weight") forms of processing (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">Singh et al., 2023)</ref>, as well as recent information-theoretic analyses of such learning trajectories of learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Conklin et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b165">Tishby and Zaslavsky, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Collectively, these considerations strongly suggest that compression and generalization must be considered at multiple levels of analysis, and with respect to different forms of use.

The effort to frame these considerations in formal, information-theoretic terms may provide a useful foundation for a more detailed, and normative understanding of how and when learning can be used to optimize the tradeoff between item versus system level complexity and, more generally, between generalization and processing capacity, that we turn to next.

The information-theoretic perspective on consolidation and automatization discussed above suggests that they present an optimization problem of their own: Replay, rehearsal and practice all allow people to actively manipulate the frequency with which they process different information, selectively increasing exposure to particular patterns of correlations relative to their incidental likelihoods in the environment.

In so doing, they allow people to actively regulate the tradeoff between generalization and processing capacity in particular domains of function, the optimization of which involves at least three closely related factors: the utility of dedicated conjunctive representations in a given domain; the time (and corresponding opportunity costs) it takes to learn these; and the temporal horizon over which that utility obtains.
Characterizing the specific forms of utility that drive these processes is beyond the scope of this article.

However, the general problem can be cast in the form of an intertemporal choice with respect to maximizing the corresponding utility: When confronted with a novel or unfamiliar task, should an agent: a) rely on the flexibility of currently available generalizable representations, that can support immediate performance in novel environments, and thus maximize utility over the short term, but that foregoes the opportunity to accrue the advantages of more dedicated representations over the longer term; or b) invest in learning dedicated representations in order to accrue those advantages as soon as possible, but at the cost of the time (and attendant opportunity costs) this will incur over the shorter term.

Recent work has begun to address this question in the context of skill acquisition, multitasking capability and planning (e.g., Agrawal et al., 2021; Petri et al., 2021; Ravi et al., 2020; Sagiv et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Recent work has begun to address this question in the context of skill acquisition, multitasking capability and planning (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Agrawal et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">Petri et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">Ravi et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Sagiv et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The current framework could be used to generalize this approach to perceptual and inference processes, which may have relevance not only for understanding the profiles of human performance, but for the design of artificial systems, a concern that we turn to next.

Progress in machine learning has produced remarkably successful systems that, in many instances, exhibit generalization abilities comparable to that of humans (e.g., in tests of analogical reasoning; Hu et al., 2023; T. Webb et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Progress in machine learning has produced remarkably successful systems that, in many instances, exhibit generalization abilities comparable to that of humans (e.g., in tests of analogical reasoning; <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Hu et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">T. Webb et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that they have acquired structured forms of representations -and, in particular, representational sharingthat support this capability for generalization.

According to our account, this predicts that despite their massive resources (processing units, parameters), these models should nevertheless be subject to constraints in processing capacity similar to those observed for humans when called upon to process novel information in parallel (i.e., without the adjunct of serial processing). 15 Consistent with this idea, it has been observed that the distributional properties of the data on which transformers are trained is, not surprisingly, important in determining what information is stored in the structure of the weights, and what information relies on dynamic construction of activity states, often referred to as "in context" learning (Chan et al., 2022).
text.formatted: According to our account, this predicts that despite their massive resources (processing units, parameters), these models should nevertheless be subject to constraints in processing capacity similar to those observed for humans when called upon to process novel information in parallel (i.e., without the adjunct of serial processing). <ref type="foot" target="#foot_11">15</ref> Consistent with this idea, it has been observed that the distributional properties of the data on which transformers are trained is, not surprisingly, important in determining what information is stored in the structure of the weights, and what information relies on dynamic construction of activity states, often referred to as "in context" learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Chan et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: More specifically, it was found that weight-based learning occurred for high frequency items involving stable correlations in the data; whereas large numbers of rarely occurring classes and/or items, the meanings of which were dynamic rather than fixed across samples, tended to rely on in context learning.

These observations align well with the idea that stable, frequently encountered forms of correlation will, with sufficient exposure, be assigned dedicated conjunctive codes and become incorporated into the system's set of existing semantic codes, with weights dedicated to the relevant correlations.
This is comparable to the processes of consolidation and automatization discussed above.

In contrast, items encountered less frequently (i.e., involving more "novel" correlations) will rely on dynamically constructed compositional representations formed from existing semantic codes; that is, the correlations will be represented using rapid binding mechanisms (in this case, in activity states; i.e., WM) similar to those used in the models described in this article.

These observations also reinforce the prediction made by our analysis, that the amount of information transformers can process using "in context" learning should be limited in ways similar to humans when they are forced to process information involving novel items comprised of correlations infrequently (or not) experienced during training.
As noted earlier, this may already be evident in large machine learning models.

For example, one recent study investigated the extent to which existing vision-language models (VLMs; such as GPT-4v) can reliably distinguish among simultaneously presented items, using the types of tasks and stimuli that have been used to characterize capacity constraints in humans, including some we have considered in this article.
That study found that VLMs consistently exhibited constraints in processing capacity as restrictive as those observed for humans forced to rely on rapid parallel processing (Campbell et al., 2024).
text.formatted: That study found that VLMs consistently exhibited constraints in processing capacity as restrictive as those observed for humans forced to rely on rapid parallel processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Campbell et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This is consistent with the supposition that VLMs rely on the learning of shared representations that are useful for generalization, and the generality of the principle that such representations should be associated with restrictions in processing capacity.

Interestingly, there is growing evidence that, when these models are augmented with mechanisms for serial processing (e.g., fine tuning on pointing, and/or use of "chain of thought"), they are better at performing such tasks, again consistent with human performance and the role of control-dependent serial processing in overcoming the constraints imposed by representations that are structured for generalization.
Finally, in a separate line of work in machine learning, there have been extensive studies seeking ways to improve the generalization performance of neural networks.

These have shown that training networks on several related tasks in ways that encourage the discovery of shared structure -referred to variously as "multitask training" (Baxter, 1995; Bengio et al., 2013; Caruana, 1997) or meta-learning (Finn et al., 2017; Hospedales et al., 2021; Santoro et al., 2016) -can substantially improve performance on novel tasks that share similar structure.
text.formatted: These have shown that training networks on several related tasks in ways that encourage the discovery of shared structure -referred to variously as "multitask training" <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Baxter, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Bengio et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Caruana, 1997)</ref> or meta-learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Finn et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Hospedales et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Santoro et al., 2016)</ref> -can substantially improve performance on novel tasks that share similar structure.

text.text: Critically, however, networks in these paradigms are only ever trained or asked to perform one task at a time.

Recently, the effects of such learning have been interpreted in terms of the acquisition of compositional representations, that favor efficiency of learning through generalization, but that this comes at the cost of dramatic restrictions in multitasking capability -the ability perform multiple tasks at the same time (Musslick et al., 2023) -an effect that is largely invariant to the size of the network (Petri et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Recently, the effects of such learning have been interpreted in terms of the acquisition of compositional representations, that favor efficiency of learning through generalization, but that this comes at the cost of dramatic restrictions in multitasking capability -the ability perform multiple tasks at the same time <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">(Musslick et al., 2023)</ref> -an effect that is largely invariant to the size of the network <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">(Petri et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Again, this is consistent with the principle that, whereas structured representations support generalization and therefore more efficient learning, this comes at the expense of processing capacity -in this case, the ability to simultaneously represent the information needed to perform multiple tasks in parallel.

As noted above, recent work has begun to consider ways in which the tradeoff between generalization and processing capacity can be optimized, using both formal analysis of abstracted networks in simple task settings (e.g., Petri et al., in press; Sagiv et al., 2018), and using deep learning in the context of more complex and realistic tasks (e.g., Ravi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: As noted above, recent work has begun to consider ways in which the tradeoff between generalization and processing capacity can be optimized, using both formal analysis of abstracted networks in simple task settings (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Petri et al., in press;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Sagiv et al., 2018)</ref>, and using deep learning in the context of more complex and realistic tasks (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">Ravi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These findings may have significance for the design of artificial systems.
Most work to date has focused on generalization: how artificial systems can achieve the efficiency of learning and flexibility afforded by generalization, and exhibited by humans.

It is widely assumed that this will require imbuing models with more powerful inductive biases for discovering structure, whether in their training curricula (e.g., Marinescu et al., 2024) and/or their architecture (e.g., T. W. Webb et al., 2024), in order to optimize the bias-variance tradeoff.
text.formatted: It is widely assumed that this will require imbuing models with more powerful inductive biases for discovering structure, whether in their training curricula (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Marinescu et al., 2024)</ref> and/or their architecture (e.g., T. W. <ref type="bibr" target="#b175">Webb et al., 2024)</ref>, in order to optimize the bias-variance tradeoff.

text.text: As discussed above, one way to frame this is the need to form dedicated representations of high frequency items that can be combined (i.e., compositionally) to represent as many low frequency items as possible.

However, while optimizing this tradeoff remains a major challenge for the design of artificial systems, the work we have presented suggests that, even with complete success in this effort, the design problem faces another tradeoff: inductive biases that maximize generalization will carry a commensurate cost in parallel processing capacity.
That is, they will be subject to the curse of generalization.

This, in turn, will require the incorporation of control mechanisms needed to serialize processing, to mitigate the risk of interference from simultaneous use of representations optimized for generalization, in just the way the human brain seems have solved this problem though the use of control-dependent processing.

This tradeoff between flexibility but inefficiency of serial processing imposed by generalizable representations, and the efficiency but more narrowly constrained applications of parallel processing afforded by task-dedicated representations is comparable to a similar tradeoff faced in traditional computational architectures, between highly flexible components (e.g., interpreted procedures and general-purpose processors) and purpose-dedicated ones (e.g., compiled procedures, drivers and custom chipsets).
It is intriguing to consider the possibility that this reflects yet another expression of the information-theoretic principles considered in this article.
Whether or not this is so, the tension is a fundamental one for any adaptive system that must function in the real world.

While flexibility and generalization are clearly assets in non-stationary, unpredictable environments, so is the need to simultaneously encode and meaningfully distinguish among multiple sources of input, and/or efficiently execute multiple independent tasks in parallel -capabilities that are likely to be critical for artificial autonomous agents in naturalistic environments.

It is clear that the human brain has developed mechanisms to adjudicate this tradeoff and, as discussed above, to adapt both its behavior and its structure over time to do so as a function of experience and need.

We hope that our consideration of the information-theoretic principles underlying this tradeoff will help advance the understanding of how this tradeoff is managed by the brain, as well as the design of artificial agents that can do so as effectively as humans.

In this article, we provided a formal characterization of a fundamental tradeoff faced by any information processing system between: generalization -the effectiveness with which previously acquired representations can be used to process new information, that is advantaged by representational sharing (a form of compression), but that comes at the cost of potential inference introduced by such sharing; and processing capacity -the amount of information that can be processed at the same time, advantaged by the use of maximally separated (i.e., dedicated conjunctive) representations, but that comes at the cost of the time and effort required for their acquisition.

We presented an analysis of this tradeoff in an abstract, information-theoretic form, and then demonstrated that the same principles are exhibited in both a simple process model, and a neurally-inspired mechanistic model of tasks that have been used to characterize human information processing capacity constraints in perception and memory.

Finally, we argued that the same principles may apply in other domains of cognitive function that exhibit similarly restrictive constraints on processing capacity, such as language, multitasking performance and control-dependent processing, and that they appear to be expressed in artificial systems as well.

Our account follows a long tradition of work that assumes natural agents place a premium on generalizable representations, both for the efficiency they afford during learning, and the flexibility they afford in novel settings.
Our analyses explored the properties of such representations in relatively simple formulations of the problem, and for relatively simple tasks that have been used in the laboratory.
The extent to which these findings themselves generalize to more complex forms of structure present in the world, and tasks that must make use of that structure, remains an open question.

However, it seems likely that similar effects will be observed in such realistic environments, given the statistical complexity of the natural world, and the value of responding flexibly and effectively within it.

At the same time, it is obvious that processing capacity can also be of considerable value, and it is clear that humans actively invest the effort to achieve this when the demand is sufficiently frequent and the consequences sufficiently valuable, through processes such as consolidation and automatization.

The information-theoretic approach we have presented offers a unifying, formally rigorous framework for understanding these processes, as the formation of purpose-dedicated, conjunctive representations that reduce the similarity with (i.e., increases the distance from) other codes with which they may interfere.

In their commentary on Miller's "magical number 7 plus or minus two," Shiffrin and Nosofsky (1994) (pg. 360) noted: ". . . the possibility that there may exist some deeper connection may have contributed to the fame of this article, despite Miller (1956) convincing and amusing arguments to the contrary.

text.text: If there is a deep connection, it continues to escape the field: The dominant theories and paradigmatic approaches in these two domains have gone their separate ways, with little, if any, cross talk."

The work we have presented here strives to bring together these different approaches, and converges on the conclusion that tempted Miller, but that he ultimately (though perhaps coyly) rejected: the consistency of capacity limits in the range of the "magic number 7" is not a coincidence.

Rather, we suggest that it is a reflection of a fundamental tradeoff between the value of generalizable representations in processing novel stimuli, and the cost this extracts in processing capacity when called upon to do so.
This tradeoff between generalization and processing capacity defines an envelope of performance that finite information processing agents can hope to achieve.

In recognition of the influence of Miller's observations, his drawing of attention to the relevant questions that persist to the present, his formal framing of the problem, and his provocative instigation of the search for a common principle, we suggest that this relationship be referred to as the Miller-Shepard Law.
