Here we elaborate on the connections between the information bottleneck (IB) and the tasks we use to operationalize and analyze the tension between the identification and generalization.

As described in the section on Task Design under Simple Process Model, a trial in each task involved sampling a set of stimuli S from a much broader space of possible stimuli; presenting a compressed representation of a probe that was drawn either from S (identification task) or a different stimulus in the same space from which S was drawn (similarity task); and responding either by identifying the member of S corresponding to the probe (identification task) or that was closest to it (generalization task).

Both of these can be viewed as forms of a categorization tasks, in which the compressed probe needs to be assigned to the correct category, i.e. the corresponding stimulus in S; and the construction of an encoder that performs categorization in an "optimal" way can be formalized using the Information Bottleneck (IB) formalism.
Thus, it is reasonable to ask how that optimization problem relates formally to the analyses of the tension between identification and generalization presented in this article.
To address this question, we first denote how the IB formalizes the categorization problem.

Let Y be a random variable taking values in a discrete set of categories and X be a random variable representing an instance of a stimulus that belongs to one of the categories, e.g. a picture of a dog. p(x|y) will thus represent the data-generating distribution.
The variable X is then compressed to X through the action of a stochastic encoder p(x|x).

The information bottleneck is defined by the optimization problem over the possible encoders p(x|x), such that the amount of information about Y contained in X (accuracy) is maximized, while minimizing the amount of information about X preserved in X (complexity): min
Here β is a compression parameter that regulates how much the maximization of accuracy is to be favored over the minimization of complexity.

We can further expand this Markov chain structure by adding an extra variable Y → X → X → Ŷ that encodes the prediction about the category Y that the agent can make starting from the compressed stimulus X. We assume that this is performed in a Bayes-optimal way by using the true posterior:
We can also take the mutual information between Y and its prediction Ŷ , I(Y ; Ŷ ), as another measure of accuracy that quantifies how much these two variables are correlated.
The data processing inequality tells us that in general I(Y ; Ŷ ) ≤ I(Y ; X), meaning that a high value of I(Y ; Ŷ ) also ensures high accuracy.
We now consider how the identification task used in our work can be formulated in similar terms.
For a given stimulus set S = (s 1 , . . . , s n ), we can define a random variable Y the value of which is the index y ∈ {1, . . . , n} of the stimulus to be identified.
The probe X is deterministically generated as p(x|y) = δ x,sy and is then compressed through the encoder p(x|x).
A prediction Ŷ is made about Y by using the same Bayes-optimal decoder of Equation (A24).
The accuracy function used in the work reported in the article is I(Y ; Ŷ ).
Thus, the resulting structure Y → X → X → Ŷ perfectly resembles the IB structure outlined above.

Accordingly, to the extent that the compression parameter β is optimized for the identification task, then the solution comports with the standard IB formulation, defining a Pareto front for the relationship between accuracy and complexity (e.g., see Figure 3B).

text.text: However, the primary focus of the work reported in this article is on a different optimization problem, in which the encoder responsible for the compression p(x|x) is optimized for the rate-distortion problem X → X. This is the Shepard-like generalization problem, formulated in terms of RDT by Sims, in which stimuli are compressed while minimizing the expected distortion given by a distortion function D:
In other words, the encoder is optimized to map similar stimuli (w.r.t.
D) in the world to nearby representations in the psychological space.
This reflects a key theoretical difference: cognitive compression is fundamentally optimized for more general-purpose representation and not for a specific task.

This pre-existing, task-independent encoder is then applied to specific tasks, such as the identification or similarity tasks used in this article, and the influence that different levels of compression parameterized by β have on performance is analyzed in each.

A second important difference from the standard IB formulation is that the set of categories, that we assumed above to be fixed, is itself the result of sampling procedure, and thus changes in each task instance (i.e., trial).
Accordingly, our analyses evaluate performance on sets of categories comprised of independently sampled stimuli, and that can also vary in size.

Note that this also includes compression of the stimuli in S → Ŝ, with the decision about the identity of the compressed probe made based on the set of compressed representations Ŝ and probe X, without direct access to S, X. A response can then be generated using a Bayes-optimal decoder, that computes the true Bayes posterior as described above.
However, this requires complex computations and does not give a closed formula in general.
Accordingly, we used a decoder p(ŷ|ŝ, x) with a simple form of Luce's law as the decision rule, that was tractable to analysis.

Finally, we note that despite the added compression step for the stimuli in S, which can only further compromise identification performance, this formulation of the identification task is functionally homologous to the one described above for fixed S, and thus the results reported in the article on the tension between identification and generalization should be qualitatively the same.
For the identification task, we constructed test sets of various sizes by uniformly sampling from the feature interval [0, 1], and randomly selecting one of the items in the set as the probe.
We then quantified the ability to identify the matching item in the set by reporting its index.

We measured performance as the mutual information between, on average, the index of the correct response (i.e., an integer from 1, . . . , N for a set size of N ) and the index of the model's response.
We computed this mutual information via a numerical simulation that estimated the joint probability distribution over the correct responses X and model's responses Y .
Thus, for set size N , the maximum possible information was log 2 N .
We explored set sizes up to 256 so that, in principle, processing capacity as measured by this task could be as high as 8 bits.

For the generalization task, we randomly selected test sets of N items from all possible items, sampled a probe item uniformly from the set of all possible items excluding any in the test set, and then quantified the ability to pick which of the N items in the test set was most similar to the probe; that is, the one closest given the distance metric applied to the features.
In the simple 1D case, there was no need to specify the form of the distance metric, under the assumption that distance is a monotonic function of the difference between the two features.
For the 2D case, we examined several distance functions, as described below.
Note, once again, that only the choice of the probe item differed between the two tasks; their structure and performance measures were otherwise equivalent.

We manipulated four primary factors to examine the tradeoff of between generalization and identification performance: 1) the generalization gradient applied to item distances (viz., the exponential decay rate β as described above, that implemented a form of compression); 2) noise in the decision process (viz., the additive term ∆ also described above); 3) set size in the generalization task N g (viz., the number of items against which the probe was compared); and 4) the dimensionality of item representations together with the distance metric used to compare them.
Note that varying N g will lead to different optimal generalization gradients that maximize performance for the corresponding set size in that task.

We also manipulated set size in the identification task N i (to evaluate processing capacity), but we focus first on results using N i = 256 (shown in Figure B1), as this provided the greatest amount of information available against which to evaluate any observed constraints in performance when compression (i.e., the generalization gradient) is optimized for the generalization task.

text.text: In contrast, compression had a non-monotonic effect on generalization and, critically, the values of β that produced the best generalization performance were associated with draconian constraints on identification performance.
These results demonstrate, once again, the tension between generalization and identification: compression that optimizes generalization severely constrains identification performance.

Note that, since the results above are based on the use of an exponential generalization gradient, and since that is optimal for compression (as discussed previously), then the solid segments of the curves in Figure B1 define a Pareto front in the tradeoff between generalization and identification performance.

text.text: Two questions that might be asked are: just how sensitive are the effects reported above to noise, and to what extent do they generalize to richer, multidimensional representations?
The latter is particularly germane to Miller's observations, which included an increase in capacity associated with the use of multidimensional stimuli in some cases.
Figure B2 addresses these questions, showing performance on the identification task evaluated over a wider range of noise levels (∆, X-axes), and 2D as well as 1D stimuli.

text.text: As in Fig -ure B1, performance for the identification task is shown for a single set size (N i = 256) providing a maximum of 8 bits of information against which performance (Z-axes) could be compared.
Each point corresponds to performance for a given level of ∆, and a value of β that optimized performance on the generalization task for a given set size (N g , Y-axes).

The black line in the left vertical plane of each panel plots identification performance when β is optimized for the identification (rather than the generalization) task, showing the upper bound on performance for a given level of noise.
Panels in the top row show identification performance as a linear function of noise, and in the lower as a logarithmic function of noise (to provide a more detailed view of the lowest levels).
The leftmost panels show the 1D case, corresponding to the mathematical analyses and simulations reported above.

At ∆ = 0, identification performance is at the optimal level of 8 bits, and is invariant to the set size N g of the generalization task for which β was optimized, since the latter was always the largest possible value (narrowest gradient); this is consistent with the results of the analyses above, indicating that in the absence of decision noise, both identification and generalization are optimized by maximizing β.

Importantly, and also consistent with those analyses, the surface reveals a "cliff" as ∆ increases past the smallest level, at which identification performance plummets, even for large generalization task set sizes (and correspondingly large β's), followed by a further but more gradual drop as N (and optimal β) decreases.
The log plots (lower row) show that these effects obtained at the very lowest levels of ∆ (down to 10 -60 ).
Furthermore, as the N for which generalization task performance is optimized (and thus β) is decreased, the surface quickly descends to within the range of 2.5-4 bits of information.
In the Appendix, Section A.3 we provide a mathematical analysis that provides insights into the shape of this surface, including the presence of the cliff.

In particular, it provides an expression for an upper bound on identification task performance as a function of noise and β optimal for various set sizes N in the generalization task -a bound that is once again tight even for very low levels of ∆.
2D items.

Finally, we explored the effect of multidimensional item representations, required for considering compositionality, and concomitantly the way in which similarity (i.e., distance) between items is measured.
The middle and rightmost panels in Figure B2 show identification task performance for 2D items.

text.text: The tasks were simulated in the same way as for 1D items, with the exception that items were comprised of a pair of features, each randomly and independently drawn from each of two orthogonal dimensions.
This, in turn, required a modification of how distances were computed.
Here we examined the implications of two of the simplest possible extensions of the measure used for the 1D case.

The middle column shows performance when distances were computed as a direct Euclidean (L2) extension of the measure used in the 1D case (i.e., the hypotenuse defined by the distances along each of the two dimensions).
The results are similar, although they show a measurable effect of higher dimensional representations: the cliff remains but the surface of identification task performance is shifted upward.

This is consistent with empirical observations, noted by Miller (1956), that processing capacity can sometimes be increased when multidimensional stimuli are used (Beebe-Center et al., 1955; Klemmer and Frick, 1953).
text.formatted: This is consistent with empirical observations, noted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Miller (1956)</ref>, that processing capacity can sometimes be increased when multidimensional stimuli are used <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Beebe-Center et al., 1955;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Klemmer and Frick, 1953)</ref>.

text.text: While Euclidean distance is a natural mathematical extension of the distance measure used for the 1D case in mathematical analyses and preceding simulations, it makes two assumptions relevant to how psychological distance may be determined in such settings.
First, it necessarily assumes that distance is measured between the conjunctive representation of each item (i.e., each as a single, unique point in the 2D space).

In our simulations, this conjunctive representation is formed by binding the features associated with each item, either by concatenating those features (simulations above), or through rapid Hebbian learning in an autoassociative (as reported in the next section).

Importantly, in both cases we assumed that this binding was temporary (i.e, restricted to the duration of the trial and/ or task), and was between features that were themselves represented along independent dimensions -that is, the binding was over features represented in a compositional form (see Figure 7), rather than the use of a dedicated, stable conjunctive code for those items.
text.formatted: Importantly, in both cases we assumed that this binding was temporary (i.e, restricted to the duration of the trial and/ or task), and was between features that were themselves represented along independent dimensions -that is, the binding was over features represented in a compositional form (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">7</ref>), rather than the use of a dedicated, stable conjunctive code for those items.

text.text: This suggests the possibility that, under such conditions, the system may not have learned how to compute distances directly between such (transient) conjunctions, and so must rely on the distances between features along each dimension over which the conjunction is composed -something that it is more likely to have been learned.
However, whereas these distances could then be used (with Pythagoras' Theorem) to explicitly compute the Euclidean distance, this seems an unlikely prospect.
Alternatively, it seems reasonable to consider the possibility of computing distances independently along each dimension, and using that information to make the relevant judgement.
Here we consider the case in which the minimum distance along either dimension is used to make the judgement (though other strategies are possible).
The results of this are shown in the rightmost panels of Figure B2.
text.formatted: The results of this are shown in the rightmost panels of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_16">B2</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to Euclidean distance, use of the minimum distance measure reduces information in the identification task relative to the 1D case.

The results of the two 2D cases reported above bracket the 1D case, suggesting that how distances are computed for higher dimensional representations can impact identification performance, and its consequences for processing capacity.
This is consistent with empirical evidence suggesting that different psychological distance functions may be used for different types of representations (Shepard, 1987).
text.formatted: This is consistent with empirical evidence suggesting that different psychological distance functions may be used for different types of representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">(Shepard, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: The theoretical observations we report here further suggest that familiarity, and how this interacts with representational dimensionality, may be an important factor.

This aligns with the general idea that consistent experience with a particular set of stimuli drives the formation of dedicated conjunctive codes (vs. ones constructed from compositional representations), and that this increases processing capacity.
This may help explain such processes as chunking, consolidation and automatization, to which we return in the General discussion).
Here, we note that this may extend not only to the conjunctive representations themselves, but to learning of an appropriate distance metric among them.

Taken together, the results from the process model simulations reinforce and extend the mathematical analyses presented in the first part of the paper, showing that with any uncertainty in a similarity-based decision process, there is a non-monotonic relationship between compression and generalization.
More specifically, the results indicate that, even with minimal amounts of decision noise, optimizing compression for generalization imposes severe constraints on the accuracy of identification.

That, in turn, takes a radical toll on processing capacity, restricting this to the range of about 2.5-4 bits -remarkably close to Miller's observation of about 2-3 bits that he canonized as the "magical number seven plus or minus two."

Note that we implemented compression as an exponential generalization gradient-the provably optimal form of compression for similarity-based generalization, ensuring that any choice of compression lies along the Pareto front in the tradeoff between compression and identification accuracy (see back plane of Figure 2).

text.text: If each of these spatial locations is equiprobable, an observation that a stimulus is located at a particular spatial position would carry 19.47 bits of information.
We therefore seek a grid-like coding scheme that scales 8 frequencies at √ e and has a representational capacity of ∼19.47 bits.
To estimate the representational capacity of a possible coding scheme, we care about the joint entropy H of the entire collection (z 1 , . . . , z L ).
The upper bound for the joint entropy is the sum of the marginal entropies.
Then, intuitively, any mutual information between nodes decreases the joint entropy of the code.
To approximate the joint entropy here, we compute the Chow-Liu estimator for the joint probability distribution (p(z 1 , . . . , z L )) over coding elements (1, . . . , L).

The Chow-Liu algorithm provides a procedure by which to select a partial set of second-order conditional probabilities and marginal probabilities to construct a maximum-weight spanning tree over variables using the pairwise mutual information between nodes as edge weights.
Specifically, the tree-structured joint entropy was estimated as where H(z) is the marginal entropy of each node i, defined as: and I(z i , z j ) is the pairwise mutual information between nodes.
The former is the total entropy if all variables were independent, which can only be reduced by the sum of selected pairwise mutual informations along the maximum-weight spanning tree.

Using this method to estimate the joint entropy, we find that a 2D array of 100x100 states encoded with a grid-like code of 8 frequencies, scaled at the √ e, and 4 phases per frequency has a joint entropy of ∼19 bits, making it a good approximation of the expected representational capacity, while respecting our desires for generalization by virtue of preserving similarity-structure.

(B) Compositional codes represent states of the world as combinations of feature values along each dimension (e.g., shape: square, color: red, x-position: 3, y-position: 3, etc.).
This provides the flexibility to process novel stimuli, by allowing any item to be represented whether or not it has previously been experienced (Fodor and Pylyshyn, 1988).

(C) Conjunctive codes assign a distinct code to each distinct item that, in the limit, is equidistant from all other codes.
While this preserves the unique identify of each item, it is an inefficient form of representation (see text).

In the neural network model, we use empirical estimates of similarity structure among feature values along a dimension to implement the distances that determine semantic structure.
Compositional structure.
While we assume that features have semantic, and thus correlational structure within each dimension, we assume that features are uncorrelated across dimensions (see Figure 7).

text.text: Accordingly, as noted above, the dimensions form a basis set for the full space, such that any state of the system can be represented as a combination of its features along each dimension.
We refer to this as compositional representation.
Also as noted above, this can be hierarchically structured.

For example, we can consider two intuitively meaningful levels of compositionality within the representation of a given state: compositionality of the representation of each item in terms of its feature values, that amounts to the concatenation of its features along each dimension (i.e., for each of the points comprising its location), and reflecting the covariation of its feature values along those dimensions; and the compositionality of items within a given state (e.g., objects in a display), that amounts to the simultaneous representation of (i.e., superposition of the codes for) feature values along each dimension belonging to the different items in that state, and reflecting the covariation of those items in physical space (i.e., the locations spanned by the display) and/or in time (i.e., their co-occurrence during the duration of the display).

Accordingly, to the extent that the identities of individual items need to be kept distinct within a state and/or different states need to be kept distinct, then there needs to be some mechanism of associating (binding) the feature values belonging to each particular item and/or the items within a state.

This is because compositionally structured representations reflect only the first order statistics of the features involved (i.e., their marginal frequencies), and not higher order statistics needed to represent correlations.
For items, this means only the (frequency with which) feature values are present in the state are represented.

This is sufficient to identify the coherent covariation of feature values that defines an individual item, but insufficient to keep these distinct for different co-occurring items; the latter requires some associative mechanism for encoding higher order statistics among feature values.
The same applies to higher level conjunctions, such as among items within an display.

The work we present points out that tasks used to study constraints in human information processing capacity are usually designed to probe item identification in settings that demand compositional representation -that is, the encoding of states that are novel compositions of items, which may themselves be novel compositions of feature values.

This demand reflects the generalizability of compositional and semantic coding, that comes at the cost of processing capacity-that is, strict constraints on the number of items that can be distinguishably represented at the same time (e.g. "set size") -that are empirically observed.
Our focus in this article is on forms of representational structure that promote generalization.
In information-theoretic terms, this can be thought of as a form of compression (e.g., Sims, 2018).

text.text: There are two primary motivations for this approach: 1) to explicitly operationalize generalization as a form of compression, not all forms of which necessarily support generalization; and 2) and quantify its effects on processing capacity.

In the following, we consider in greater detail the relationship between this operationalization of generalization, the forms of representational structure outlined above, and standard information-theoretic constructs.
Probabilistic vs. similarity structure.
If the world had no structure, then the only way to represent it would be by pairing each state with a unique code.

That is, there would be no opportunity for generalization, and the agent would obligately face the curse of dimensionality, manifest in the number of samples (and hence time) required to learn such a code. 23 Fortunately, however, the world does appear to have structure, and thus the curse of dimensionality can be mitigated through the acquisition and use of more efficient forms of coding that support generalization.
text.formatted: That is, there would be no opportunity for generalization, and the agent would obligately face the curse of dimensionality, manifest in the number of samples (and hence time) required to learn such a code. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_17">23</ref> Fortunately, however, the world does appear to have structure, and thus the curse of dimensionality can be mitigated through the acquisition and use of more efficient forms of coding that support generalization.

text.text: Traditional work on efficient coding in information theory (e.g., Barlow, 1961; Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006), and its application to learning and representation (Friston, 2010; Linsker, 1988; Tishby et al., 2000), have focused largely on one particular form of structure: the probability distribution over states of the world.
text.formatted: Traditional work on efficient coding in information theory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Barlow, 1961;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006)</ref>, and its application to learning and representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Linsker, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">Tishby et al., 2000)</ref>, have focused largely on one particular form of structure: the probability distribution over states of the world.

text.text: Accordingly, they have been driven by a fundamental tenet of information theory: that efficiency of coding can be maximized by optimizing complexity to reflect probabilistic structure.

More specifically, the complexity (e.g., number of bits) of a code assigned to a state should be proportional to its surprisal (the negative log probability of its occurrence), so that shorter codes are used to represent more frequent states.

There are at least two ways in which this can be thought of as efficient: i) it minimizes the average complexity of the system's representations for a given level of mutual information between those and the potential states of the world, by minimizing the resources (e.g., total number of bits) needed to represent those states given their likelihoods; it maximizes rate which, in RDT, is defined as the number of bits required to transmit a signal on average: using fewer bits for the most frequent signals means more efficient transmission (fewer bits per signal) on average.
The latter also has implications for rate in another sense: how much information can be transmitted per unit time, assuming a channel capacity that imposes some requirement for serial processing.

The latter bears a close relationship to the construct of processing capacity on which we have focused -how many signals can be reliably represented and transmitted at the same time -although, as noted this is not usually how the problem is framed, at least not in the context of cognitive science, neuroscience or machine learning applications (see Note 1).
The idea that the frequency of a state should impact how it is represented has played a central role in statistically-motivated theories of representational learning.

While these do not always formulate the relationship explicitly in terms of complexity or efficiency, they do address how factors such as passive experience, replay, rehearsal and practice -mediated by psychological processes such as consolidation (e.g., Kumaran et al., 2016; McClelland et al., 1995) and automatization (Anderson, 1983; Musslick et al., 2023; Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977) -can lead information that is processed more frequently to be represented more compactly.
text.formatted: While these do not always formulate the relationship explicitly in terms of complexity or efficiency, they do address how factors such as passive experience, replay, rehearsal and practice -mediated by psychological processes such as consolidation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Kumaran et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">McClelland et al., 1995)</ref> and automatization <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Anderson, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Musslick et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977)</ref> -can lead information that is processed more frequently to be represented more compactly.

text.text: The same may be true for longer term processes, such as evolution and/or early development.

In the Discussion we consider how this relationship between frequency and representational structure might be considered within an information theoretic framework, and in particular with regard to the tension between generalization and processing capacity (see Overcoming Capacity Constraints, and Conjunctive Codes: Recoding, Automatization, and Consolidation).

However, our primary focus in this article is not on how the system can most efficiently represent or process the most frequent states, but rather on how it accommodates the need to process the most infrequent states -that is, ones statistically out of the distribution of prior experience -which demand generalization, and how that impacts efficiency.

Infrequent states can be ones comprised of items with novel or unfamiliar features (i.e., semantically unusual states), and/or novel combinations of features or items (i.e., compositionally unusual states).

Note, however, that while instances of such states may individually be infrequent, encountering infrequent states as a class may be common, especially in high dimensional, non-stationary -i.e., naturalistic -environments.
Accordingly, the effectiveness with which infrequent states can be processed is critical to adaptation.

Furthermore, the processing of such states is assumed to rely on mechanisms responsible for the flexibility of processing (e.g., working memory and cognitive control), and tasks used to study these mechanisms are therefore designed specifically to elicit such states -that is, ones that involve the processing of unfamiliar items, such as ones comprised of novel combinations of features (e.g., colors, shapes and positions as shown in Figure 1A).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the processing of such states is assumed to rely on mechanisms responsible for the flexibility of processing (e.g., working memory and cognitive control), and tasks used to study these mechanisms are therefore designed specifically to elicit such states -that is, ones that involve the processing of unfamiliar items, such as ones comprised of novel combinations of features (e.g., colors, shapes and positions as shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: The primary point of this article is to argue that, precisely because these tasks are intended to tap mechanisms responsible for the flexibility of processing, and therefore rely on the capacity for generalization, they necessarily showcase the limits to human information processing capacity that reflect the curse such generalization.

Theories of optimal coding do not generally address this consequence of generalization: they prescribe how to assign codes to individual signals, based on their frequency of occurrence, but not how these should relate to codes used for other signals (e.g., semantically or compositionally).
In fact, as formalized by the Singleton Bound (Singleton, 1965), they prescribe the use of codes that are as distinct (i.e. as far) from one another as possible.
text.formatted: In fact, as formalized by the Singleton Bound <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">(Singleton, 1965)</ref>, they prescribe the use of codes that are as distinct (i.e. as far) from one another as possible.

text.text: That is, each state of the world should be assigned a unique code that is as distinct as possible, maximizing the reliability of transmission.

We refer to these as conjunctive codes, because they are arbitrary mappings to states that reflect only the unique conjunction of feature values or items that comprise a given state, and bear no systematic relation to one another.

However, under the assumption that the world has semantic and/or compositional structure outlined above, it is inefficient to represent the world in this way -both with respect to the efficiency of learning and representation.

As noted in the main text, the number of samples required to learn to represent every possible state of the world individually (i.e., as conjunctive codes) grows exponentially with the number of feature values and dimensions in the world.
In contrast, the number of samples needed to acquire a strictly compositional code grows linearly with the number of feature values and dimensions.

Thus, compositional representations of states can be acquired and represented more efficiently than conjunctive ones; and, once acquired, they can be used more flexibly to represent any possible -but as yet unexperienced -state.

Similarly, semanticity allows responses to novel states to be similar to those that share similar feature values along the behavioral relevant dimensions (and, conversely, compressing ones that are not relevantly distinct into a single representation).

Together, these maximize generalization -the ability to accurately represent and/or respond appropriately to states that have not previously been encountered, based on existing representations of ones that are similar (Shepard, 1987).
text.formatted: Together, these maximize generalization -the ability to accurately represent and/or respond appropriately to states that have not previously been encountered, based on existing representations of ones that are similar <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">(Shepard, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: However, they come at the cost of the ability to reliably identify distinct individual states, which is the criterion for performance in standard information theoretical analyses (e.g., the mutual information between the transmitted and received code).
This is because introducing similarity structure increases the potential for confusion among codes, making them harder to distinguish when that is required.

To isolate the effects of such structure, independent of probabilistic structure, the work we report in this article makes the assumption that all states are equiprobable, and represented within the system with equal complexity.

We then quantify the relationship between complexity (or, conversely, compression) and generalization, and ask how optimizing for generalization impacts identification error and, concomitantly, processing capacity.

Furthermore, this should be greatly exacerbated when multiple novel items must be represented at the same timethat is, it should reduce processing capacity.

This is evident in the Illustrative Example presented at the beginning of this article (see Figure 1), where representing novel stimuli (e.g., a yellow square next to a green square each in an arbitrary position) requires the use of compositional coding, both for items in terms of their features, and the display in terms of those items.

text.text: However, this poses a problem: without some mechanism for associating each point in the display, and similarly each item with its corresponding set of features, it would be impossible to determine which particular features belong to a given item -for example, to distinguish it from the case in which the green square was in the upper right corner, and the yellow square was below it.
That is, the use of compositional representations restricts the number of items that can be represented and identified at the same time.
This has been referred to as the "Binding Problem" in cognitive science (e.g., Treisman and Gelade, 1980).
text.formatted: This has been referred to as the "Binding Problem" in cognitive science (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">Treisman and Gelade, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: This highlights the limitations of compositionality -that is, the curse of generalizationclassically observed as a cost in the ability to identify the features of a specified item in a display containing multiple items, that increases with the number of items.

This cost is observed either as an increase in response time with the number of items, indicative of reliance on serial processing (Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977; Treisman and Gelade, 1980), or a reduction in accuracy under pressure to respond immediately (i.e, enforcing parallel processing) or after a delay (enforcing that the display be encoded in memory).
text.formatted: This cost is observed either as an increase in response time with the number of items, indicative of reliance on serial processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">(Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">Treisman and Gelade, 1980)</ref>, or a reduction in accuracy under pressure to respond immediately (i.e, enforcing parallel processing) or after a delay (enforcing that the display be encoded in memory).

text.text: This is because strictly compositional codes (i.e., without any binding) carry information only about the fist order statistics of features in a state (which are present or absent), and not higher order statistics (i.e., their associations with one another, or patterns of covariation).

The problem is exacerbated by semanticity, in which the similarity of codes for similar features makes the ability to distinguish such codes more sensitive to perturbation (e.g., if the squares had subtly different shades of yellow).
The constraints that such structured representations place on processing efficiency can be mitigated in one of two ways.

One way to overcome the constraints imposed by structured representations on the simultaneous representation of multiple items is to serialize processing, isolating each item from interference introduced by the others.
For example, the classic binding problem can be averted by using eye movements and/or attention to sequentially process items one at a time, focusing on its features in isolation of others.

A large and longstanding body of empirical evidence suggests that this is exactly what people do (e.g., Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977; Treisman and Gelade, 1980), and has been variously interpreted as the function of attention (Kahneman and Treisman, 1984) and cognitive control (Botvinick et al., 2001).

This highlights one of the most important consequences of the Miller-Shepard Law: the tension between between the flexibility of processing afforded by generalization, and the cost in processing capacity that this incurs due to the reliance on serial, control-dependent processing.
text.formatted: This highlights one of the most important consequences of <ref type="bibr">the Miller-Shepard Law:</ref> the tension between between the flexibility of processing afforded by generalization, and the cost in processing capacity that this incurs due to the reliance on serial, control-dependent processing.

text.text: This, in turn, points to a second, equally important consequence: the need to balance the value of generalization against the value of processing capacity, that can increased through representational modification.
Representational modification.
While serial processing can be used to avert the cost of identification error with structured, generalizable codes, another way to do so is to modify existing representations and/ or create new ones.

For example, distinctions between features can be made finer along relevant dimensions (by narrowing the generalization gradient) to mitigate interference due to semanticity; and/or by adding new conjunctive representations dedicated to specific combinations of features to mitigate interference due to compositionality.

As discussed above, and in the main text (see Conjunctive Codes: Recoding, Automatization and Consolidation in the Discussion), such modifications can occur through representational learning over longer time frames.

However, such longterm adaptation can't explain the flexibility people exhibit in representing and processing novel states that, by definition, have not had a chance to exert such pressure on the representations.

Rather, over the short term, it requires either rapidly binding features along different dimensions of a compositional code (i.e., to represent higher order statistics), and/or dynamically modifying the precision with which features are represented along a given dimension.
The former is the function ascribed to episodic memory by Complementary Learning Systems Theory (McClelland et al., 1995).
text.formatted: The former is the function ascribed to episodic memory by Complementary Learning Systems Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(McClelland et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: This aligns closely with binding mechanisms used in the models described in this article.

However, our findings suggest that rapid binding can only partially mitigate the constraints on processing capacity imposed by compositionalityowing in large measure to the additional effects of semanticity.
In principle, the latter could be mitigated by increasing precision.

However: i) it has been argued that this too is subject to constraints (e.g., Bays and Husain, 2008; Wilken and Ma, 2004); and ii) our analyses suggest that the degree of precision needed to overcome these constraints is extreme (see Figures A3 and B2).
text.formatted: However: i) it has been argued that this too is subject to constraints (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Bays and Husain, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b180">Wilken and Ma, 2004)</ref>; and ii) our analyses suggest that the degree of precision needed to overcome these constraints is extreme (see Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">A3</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_16">B2</ref>).

text.text: Importantly, the constraints on processing capacity observed in these analyses appear to be robust to the forms of generalization, multidimensional representations, binding mechanisms, and relevant model parameters (such as decision noise and set size) we have explored.

Nevertheless, whether and how processing constraints vary for other forms of generalization and binding mechanisms, and how this interacts with the dimensionality and compositionality of representations remain important questions for future research, some of which we consider in the Discussion.

Here we present a simple numerical simulation of the identification and generalization tasks introduced above, extending these to explore the impact of multi-dimensional representations required for compositionality, and systematically visualizing the effect of decision noise and set size (in the generalization task) that determine the optimal generalization gradients.
There are two key results.

First, we show that, once again, even for extremely low levels of noise -at which a generalization gradient can be found that achieves nearoptimal performance on the identification task -optimizing the generalization gradient for the generalization task still dramatically constrains performance on the identification task.

Second, multidimensional representations can either ameliorate or exacerbate the effect of set size on performance on the identification task, and thus processing capacity, in ways that depend on the choice of the psychological distance function in multidimensional spaces required for compositional representation.
As above, we consider the simple setting in which items have features that take continuous values in the interval [0, 1].

We consider both the 1-dimensional (1D) case, as in the mathematical analyses above, and a 2-dimensional (2D) case that allowed us to explore the use of compositional representations as well as different distance metrics.

For the 2D case, we made the simplifying assumption that there were no errors in binding the features along each dimension together into items; each item representation was a reliable concatenation of two feature values, one along each dimension.
We explore more psychologically and neurally informed mechanisms for binding in the next section, using simulations of an auto-associative network for implementing compositionality.

We implemented the two tasks described in the previous section to quantify identification and generalization performance: i) an identification task, requiring the selection of the item among a set of test items that was identical to a probe, drawn randomly from among the test items; and ii) a generalization task, requiring the selection of the item in the test set that was most similar to a probe drawn from outside the set of test items.
Items were defined by features along either a single dimension or each of two dimensions, and distances between items was computed using one of two distance metrics that we describe further below.

We modeled both tasks as a probabilistic retrieval of items from the test set given the probe, in which the probability of retrieval of each item was a normalization of the values resulting from applying the exponential generalization gradient function to the probe-item distances and, critically, perturbed by noise parameterized by ∆ as described above.

The analyses and models presented in the main text assume that there is structure in the world that our perceptual and representational apparatus have evolved to exploit, and that states of the world can be described in terms of this structure.
We elaborate on those assumptions here.

Specifically, we assume this structure can be captured by describing the world as points in a multidimensional vector space, with each point described by a vector comprised of a set of subvectors (or "fields"), each of which represents a single feature value along one of the dimensions (including location and time).
Furthermore, dimensions are assumed to be orthogonal to one another so that, over the entire space, the feature values along any given dimension vary fully independently of those along any other.
21 Accordingly, the dimensions comprise a basis set for the space, and any point in the space can be compositionally coded as a set of the feature values along each dimension.

We further define two types of hierarchically-related subspaces, that are relevant to the information processing demands of physical agents: states, that are for every point in physical space (i.e., along the three dimensions of position) and a given point (or set of points) in time, the feature values along all other dimensions; and items within a state (e.g., objects within a display, or a display within the broader scope of the state), that are comprised of a subset of points in physical space and/or time that share covariance structure across other feature dimensions (e.g., color, shape, etc.) that is independent of any other such subset.

For example, an item in Figure 1 of the main text (i.e., one of the colored shapes) can be defined as the locations in the display that all comprise the same shape (square) and share a given color (e.g., yellow), as shown in Figure E1, Panel B. 22 Critically, we assume that all of the feature values of each item, and all the items in a state are represented using the same set of codes.

Figure E1.
Types of codes.

(A)Semantic codes represent feature values that are similar along a given dimension (e.g., red x and orange y) with codes that are themselves more similar (i.e., comparably close to one another, such as x * and y * ) than they are to others (e.g., blue z).

This supports generalization(Shepard, 1987), by allowing similar feature values (e.g., red and orange) to be processed in similar ways (e.g., if it is known that red berries are poisonous, then it might be advisable to avoid eating orange ones, but perhaps less so for blue ones).
text.formatted: This supports generalization<ref type="bibr" target="#b145">(Shepard, 1987)</ref>, by allowing similar feature values (e.g., red and orange) to be processed in similar ways (e.g., if it is known that red berries are poisonous, then it might be advisable to avoid eating orange ones, but perhaps less so for blue ones).

text.text: However, for the same reason, it makes distinguishing items less reliable if they have feature values that are more similar (e.g., x and y) than different (e.g., x and z).
(B) Compositional codes represent states of the world as combinations of feature values along each dimension (e.g., shape: square, color: red, x-position: 3, y-position: 3, etc.).
This provides the flexibility to process novel stimuli, by allowing any item to be represented whether or not it has previously been experienced(Fodor and Pylyshyn, 1988).
text.formatted: This provides the flexibility to process novel stimuli, by allowing any item to be represented whether or not it has previously been experienced<ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Fodor and Pylyshyn, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: However, if there is no additional mechanism that binds the feature values of distinct items (shown here as lines connecting feature values across dimensions), then it is impossible to determine which features belong to which items.
(C) Conjunctive codes assign a distinct code to each distinct item that, in the limit, is equidistant from all other codes.
While this preserves the unique identify of each item, it is an inefficient form of representation (see text).
We use the terms "shared" and "separated" to characterize the structure of representations.

text.text: Typically, compositional representations are assumed to lie along distinct, or what Shepard 1991 called "separable" dimensions, which should be distinguished from our use of the term "separated representations."
text.formatted: Typically, compositional representations are assumed to lie along distinct, or what Shepard 1991 called "separable" dimensions, which should be distinguished from our use of the term "separated representations."

text.text: Shepard's use of "separable" refers to the dimensions along which features are representation.

If separable dimensions are used to implement compositionality (as shown in Figure7B), then the representations of items formed from these may be shared, insofar as two items that have the same feature value along a given dimension (e.g., red) make use of the same representation of that feature value (i.e., along the color dimension).

In contrast, if integral dimensions are used, then by definition their representations will be separated, insofar as each will be assigned a distinct representation, despite having a nominal feature in common.
Accordingly, we refer to these as separated representations.
Thus, the use of separable dimensions for compositionality produces shared representations, whereas the use of integral dimensions produces separated representations.
text.formatted: Thus, the use of separable dimensions for compositionality produces shared representations, whereas the use of integral dimensions produces separated representations.
